Oṃ. Salutations to Śambhu, whose form is the self-awareness of one's own vibration.
Now follow the *Spandakārikās*, accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.
The first outflow:

That whose nature is the light of consciousness, unconditioned by the ten directions, time, and so forth, which always flashes forth as the experiencer of its own such-like self; [that is the first outflow].
Śambhu’s own nature is the supreme Śākta reality, overflowing with incomparable wonder;

it triumphs in the world as *spanda* (vibration). The functions of space and so forth, because their expansion has not yet emerged within that power, are incapable of appearing as distinct entities in their own right; for even power itself exists only through its orientation toward the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).

With only the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) remaining, it is embraced by the mere radiance of the nature of the experiencer. For this very reason, the first quarter [of the verse] refers to the Possessor of Power (*śaktimān*), whose body is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) unmeasured by the conceptualization of directions and so forth. By means of the remainder [of the verse], the meaningfulness of the word "vibration" (*spanda*) is revealed.

The manifestation of the Power (*śakti*), which is inherent in that [Supreme Being] and possesses its attributes—synonymous with *brahman*, *āhlāda* (bliss), and so forth—is here perceived as the unfolding of Śakti. Through the term "is victorious" (*jayati*), the state of possessing absolute pre-eminence belonging to the Śākta reality (*śāktatattva*) is understood. Consequently, for those devoted ones who plunge into and savor the essence of immersion (*samāveśa*) therein, [this state is realized].
This implies his fitness as a vessel for the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as his desirability to the entire universe. || 1 ||
Some, entering on their own a path that is naturally dense and difficult— without having been shown the direction by those who know it—
may wander; but that they, by that very same ruined path, invite others to travel is a great delusion.
For those who plunge into the naturally profound ocean of the Śaiva Āgamas without the true tradition taught by the wise— whose consciousness is veiled by the power known as Vāmā,
and who harbor presumptions based on their own inventions— they find themselves midway, having failed to reach the further shore in reality.

[It is as if they are already submerged. Alas, for those followers who wander upon his evil path, this exhortation intended to show them the further shore is like opening one's eyes only to fall into a blind well. Therefore, this effort of mine is directed toward helping such people cross over to the other side. || 2 ||

The ocean of the scriptures is agitated by those who produce continuous, violent streams of sound that tear at the ears— streams resulting from the terrible, incessant collisions of the gales of various doctrines.

By those [commentaries], through the impetuosity of their exposition, the seeker of truth was rescued— [a seeker] whose mind was distressed by the loss of the raft of the meaning of the scriptures due to the terrifying confusion of rising whirlpools.
Some, having diverse tastes, even while knowing the supreme reality, fall into error;
another, whose intellect is obstructed by the darkness of hatred, does so by his very nature; and yet another is simply dull-witted.
Thus, a collection of words that captures the hearts of all is indeed difficult to find; nevertheless, these people today are discerning.
There are a few here who are worthy recipients for the virtuous.

Having unified the *Spandārthasūtrāvalī*— which was composed by someone else according to tradition, though it had been compiled from various sources and arranged as a double-thread by some with the intent of expansion— I [have now] set it forth.
I place this *dvayī* (the pair of works) within the rubies of the minds of the wise—pierced by the diamond-pointed power of the Lord’s grace—in order to make it fruitful.
First, the lineage of *sūtras* was obtained by the venerable Vasuguptapāda; thereafter, it was [elucidated] by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) such as the venerable Bhaṭṭakallaṭa and others.

It has been refined by the exposition of the concealed meaning; now, however, it is endowed with a distinguished composition that unifies and joins the *Spandakārikās* and the *Sūtrāvalī*, incorporates an explanation of the meaning in accordance with the commentaries (*vṛtti*),
and determines the ultimate truth as handed down in the traditional scriptures (*āgama*).

It is composed within the pure jewel-like minds of the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), which have been pierced by the crest-flame of the gem of the agitation known as the descent of supreme power (*parā-śaktipāta*). Having ascended the midst of the nectar-filled palace of Lord [Abhinavagupta] by means of the description of its fragrance, beauty, and other qualities, [this work is established].
The experience of unsurpassed bliss is relished through a mental state that has blossomed without obstruction. || 5 ||
We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), whose opening and closing of his eyes cause the dissolution and arising of the universe. || 1 ||

We praise—that is, we extol—that Śaṅkara, the creator of ultimate welfare. Who is he? He whose opening and closing—the expansion and dissolution of his power—are the destruction and manifestation of the universe, that is, of the world. Here, a correspondence between the order of terms is not intended.
We shall explain it. Of what nature is that? It is "the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers" (śakticakravibhavaprabhava).
The "wheel" (cakra) of the powers—whose essential natures will be described—is the collection itself; that very thing is the manifestation.

But how is the consistency of the subject matter (*vastusaṃgati*) to be understood? This must be investigated. Śaṅkara, being eternal, of a single unchanging nature, and the one and only ontological category, is the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*); such is the purport of this treatise, since it is established accordingly. [Yet,] his [attributes of] closing and opening, consisting of the nature of blinking, are mutually contradictory and impermanent.

How can these two specific states be presented as being in a relationship [with the Lord]? For by this very expression of agency, it is presented thus: "Śaṅkara opens his eyes and closes his eyes. And since such a connection with impermanent states is untenable in the eternal Blessed One, how was that stated?

Regarding the phrase "by whose opening and closing," it is said here: by the two words "opening" (unmeṣa) and "closing" (nimeṣa), which function metaphorically, the single will of Śaṅkara alone is expressed; and that is his eternal attribute.
Its [the world's] being the very nature [of the Lord], its being denoted by the terms "opening" and "closing," and its duality (p.
5) are [only] metaphorical, because the world itself consists of effects brought forth by the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord and is therefore impermanent.

When the occurrence of dissolution and emergence exists, closing (nimeṣa) and opening (unmeṣa) truly come into being. Since these two are caused solely by the will of the Lord (īśvara), the will of the Lord itself is metaphorically designated by the term "opening" because it is the cause of the emergence that constitutes creation, and by the term "closing" because it is the cause of the dissolution that constitutes withdrawal— just as [the cause of longevity] is [metaphorically called] "life."

By the word *āyuḥ* (life), clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is meant. And that [butter] is the power (*śakti*) of Śaṅkara, inseparable from him; and the very comprehension of that is the cause for the attainment characterized by the recognition of the Lordship of the Self (*ātmaiśvaryapratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, according to the principle to be stated in the verse "She [the Power], like the desire to see, [perceives] all objects" (Ni. 3.11), she resembles the desire well-known among worldly persons.
It is designated by the word "will" (icchā) because it is the means for its comprehension. For just as, in a person's state of will,

the object being willed exists without any deviation from its own essential nature, so too the world— variegated by the diversity of infinite manifestations— exists within the power of the Lord without deviating even in the slightest from His own essential nature, which has not undergone any modification.
It remains thus. This very state of Śiva, which is real in the ultimate sense, is praised by those who know it as follows:
"To him whose constant diversion is creation, and who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance... (p. 6).
Salutations to the Lord, who is eternally satisfied by devouring the three worlds.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"And this intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), which is manifested as the sequence of various objects, is that Great Lord, the subject whose nature is non-sequential and infinite consciousness."

Thus, the designations of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) belong to this very single power of the Supreme Lord; they arise solely from the power of *māyā* as it unfolds through the limitation of "this-ness" (*idantā*). For, apart from the singular state of Śiva, the power of *māyā* has established its footing everywhere, by virtue of which [distinctions such as] Sadāśiva and the rest appear within the single, ultimately real Śiva-principle.

This will be established during the commentary on the verse beginning with *ni0 14 kā0*. This very power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*), characterized in such a manner, is metaphorically designated as "dual" because it is the cause of the two states of the universe manifested through its own play (*līlā*).
Therefore, this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here in the first half of the opening verse: [of Him] by whose mere will the universe...

We praise that [Lord] who is both dissolution and emergence. Furthermore, in this context, the literal numerical correspondence need not be strictly observed; rather, the meaning of the number is such that emergence occurs through *unmeṣa* (expansion) and dissolution through *nimeṣa* (contraction).

It comes together. And this—namely, that the opening and closing [of the eyes] are merely a matter of will (icchāmātra)—has been explained by Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa himself, the author of the commentary, in order to establish this much as the intended meaning:
"by mere volition" (saṃkalpamātreṇa).

Thus [it is said]. However, those who—out of a desire to justify the correspondence of the sequence [of attributes]—explain that upon His *unmeṣa* (opening), due to the withdrawal of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), there is the dissolution or destruction of the world through the expansion of His own nature; and upon His *nimeṣa* (closing), due to the manifestation of the power of action, there is the emergence or arising of the world through the contraction of His own nature, [they refer] to Śaṅkara alone.

Those who establish the ultimate opening and closing (*unmeṣa-nimeṣa*) as being the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), yet understand a merely conceptual object to be the ultimate truth— have they not, indeed, entered into the inner core of this very vision? Homage to them!

But surely, since the Lord’s power is also established as being of such a nature—possessing a single, eternal, and non-deviating essence—due to the acceptance of the non-difference between the two, how can it be explained that there is a "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*)?
To this we reply: indeed, this very [power] is that unsurpassed [reality].
p.

8) By "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*) here is intended that which belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*), which is inlaid with various manifestations expanding without limit, even though there is no deviation from the mere self-reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*) in all things.
This [world], which sketches the painting of the three realms, even while being thus sketched, does not differ in the slightest from its own nature when it is ultimately investigated as such.
As it has been said:
Victorious is Your unprecedented state of supreme lordship, O Lord of All, which is devoid of anything to be ruled;
and likewise victorious is Your other [state], by which this world appears as it does, yet does not truly appear.
Thus it is written elsewhere as well:
"Homage to Śambhu, who manifests the wondrous painting of the three worlds, proclaiming his marvelous creative intuition (pratibhā),
and who shines with hundreds of illuminations drawn by the brush of his own perfectly white and subtle power."

Thus, this kind of Śiva-like sovereignty is self-evident only to those great-souled ones who are thoroughly awakened, for whom the entire darkness of *māyā* has been swallowed up by His grace and the ultimate reality has been revealed. But for those awakened by the descent of the Lord’s power (*īśvara-śaktipāta*), it is perfectly [evident].

By practicing according to the sequence of instructions from a proximate true guru, one attains immediate personal experience; however, those who are unawakened are simply not fit for instruction. This very point [is as follows]: (p. 9)
This will be established further on below. Thus, such being the case regarding the supreme sovereignty of Śaṅkara,

these infinite manifestations of entities— which, though divided into two classes as conscious and unconscious by virtue of His most wonderful power of *māyā*, are further subdivided into endless varieties— are in reality nothing but that single power which is non-different from the essential nature of the Supreme Lord.

However, appearing through the differentiation of various names and forms— which arises solely from the distinction of the reflective awareness "this"— and thus being designated as a plurality, it is called the "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*). Furthermore, when individual entities are designated by the word "power," it is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating their non-difference from the Supreme Lord, the possessor of power.

[He] employs [these]. These very [powers] are the manifestations (*vibhava*), the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), because he possesses the nature of manifesting himself in such a way through them alone. As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*)—these two are said to be the categories of reality."
The entire universe is his power, and Maheśvara is the possessor of that power.

Thus, this is the source—the cause of origination—of this manifestation which constitutes his own power; it is not [the source] of something distinct from his essential nature that has acquired its being from some other external source. And for this reason, by the words "of whom," and so forth...

Although the first half of the first verse establishes Śaṅkara as the cause of the world, the second half of the verse beginning with "tam" is not redundant; rather, its purpose is to convey a specific qualification, namely that he is the source of the world which consists of his own sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) in the form of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra*). This very point was stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*:
The state of sovereignty over the wheels of power (*śakticakra*), which consists of the body of consciousness (*vijñānadeha*), has been explained as the cause of its arising.
By such statements as these, the intended meaning is as follows: "The body of consciousness" refers to Maheśvara, whose form consists solely of pure awareness (*viśuddha-saṃvinmātra*).

He is the "Self" (*ātman*), that is, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) which consists of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*). Furthermore, he in whom such attributes are invariably present is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is designated by the term *Śaṃkara* according to the meaning that will be explained.
This has been established here (p.
that which is indicated by the pronouns "he" and "that" in the construction of the sentence suggests that he is indeed the Self and nothing else.

By reflecting upon the meaning of the section elaborated in these fifty verses, it is established that the aforementioned qualification applies exclusively to that [Self] which is of the nature of Śiva. This very point has been demonstrated by the author of the Vṛtti through this [verse], regarding one's own essential nature as being Śiva.

By explaining it thus, he intends the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of his own [term] *sva* to be: "one's own" (*ātmanaḥ svaḥ*); "one's own state" (*ātmīyo bhāvaḥ*), that is, one's own form (*svarūpam*), which is one's own nature (*svasvabhāvaḥ*). Therefore, the intended essential meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of this first verse—which consists in the formulation of the promise regarding the subject matter to be sustained throughout the treatise—is as follows: the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaraḥ*).

By mere will, He brings about the dissolution and emergence of the universe; although the universe has attained its stability, it is solely the manifestation of His power (*śakti-vibhūti*), yet through the influence of *māyā*, it appears as manifold. These two points alone are elaborated upon in this section by means of a sequence of logical arguments and empirical evidence. And so:

Precisely because, due to the power of *māyā*, there is from the very beginning no emergence of the reflective awareness of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-pratyavamarśa*), [the self] appears as non-different from the objects of knowledge, such as the body and so forth.

The distinction from the Self is demonstrated; therefore, the world, which is the object of cognition, is non-distinct from that cognizer whose true nature has been realized, by virtue of existing as its power (*śakti*). Thus, by this verse, the *Spanda* doctrine—the fourfold outflow consisting of reasoning and perception regarding these two very points—is set forth as a sūtra.

And its status as a *siddhānta* (established conclusion) belongs only to that which is already established—not to that which is yet to be proven—since it is the finality, the culmination, and the certainty regarding the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*). Alternatively, it is the status of a *siddhānta* belonging precisely to this [text] consisting of knowledge and action, which has been proclaimed in various *siddhāntas*. Furthermore, it serves the purpose of ensuring the completion of the commenced section without obstacles.

The teachers indicate that even the relationship (*saṃbandha*) and other elements are suggested by the first verse; this is understood from the very phrase "we praise all that which is Śaṃkara. For [the former] is the means (*upāya*), characterized as the scripture of the highest good (*śreyaḥ-śāstra*), while [the latter] is primarily the goal (*upeya*), characterized as the recognition of the sovereignty of the Self (*ātmaiśvarya-pratyabhijñā*).
Both of these are expressed by the word *śam*; its author is Śaṅkara, and thus this name is etymologically significant.

[This is] of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is the direct author of this auspiciousness which consists of this scripture. Those who have composed this tradition [of the scripture] have received the designation of "author. Thus, there is a relationship between the Lord and the scripture characterized by that of agent and work. Regarding the subject matter here, we praise it as the true nature of Śaṅkara, based on the word "we praise" (stumaḥ).

It is understood that the very purpose of praise is the elucidation of the nature of the object to be attained; this is indeed certain for the wise. Therefore, the relationship between the scripture and its subject matter is characterized by that of the signifier and the signified. And the purpose consists in the recognition of one's own sovereignty, which arises from the very word of Śaṅkara.
It is determined that even for another who acts for the sake of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), it is indeed Īśvara who is explained [as the agent].
Thus, the relationship between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) is characterized by the nature of the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*).
In this way, the three—relationship and so forth—have been explained. The designation of this treatise is *Spanda*, because [it exists] for the sake of discerning the reality of *spanda*.
In such passages as [Tantrāloka] 1.21.2, the conventional usage is precisely this. Furthermore, this term *spanda* refers to the mere self-reflection of one's own essential nature.

The Supreme Lord’s attribute— consisting of a mere intensity of effort, which serves as the cause for the exclusion of emptiness from that which is eternal, and which is designated by the other name "power"— is termed *spanda* (vibration) because it denotes its own meaning through even a slight movement; and since this treatise is the means for explaining that [attribute], it too is designated by the word *spanda*.

It is explained as follows: regarding the term "subject" (*viṣaya*), in other treatises the word "subject" refers to the topic of instruction—that is, the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*). However, here the intended meaning of "subject" is that which is to be expressed (*abhidheya*), which has already been previously explained.
Of this...

For one whose innate consciousness is being awakened by the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*)—a descent indicated by the excellence of pure faith and devotion—and who has received the purificatory rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) properly bestowed, the realization of the sovereignty of one's own self remains dependent solely on the impulsion of the Guru’s word;
for it is precisely such a person who was previously accepted here as the fit recipient of instruction. Thus, both the name and its object [have been explained].
These two are to be understood. And this opening verse has been explained as containing within it the introduction to the entire subject matter of the treatise. || 1 ||

Indeed, [this is evident] from the diversity of the multitude of living beings—distinguished by their bodies, organs, and activities according to the divisions of gods, humans, animals, and so forth—and from the variety of their experiences such as pleasure, pain, hunger, thirst, and the like. (p. 15)

How can that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which is mutually and distantly distinct be asserted as non-different from Śaṅkara, who possesses the marvelous sovereignty just described? By what [reasoning] has this been explained? How could he whose non-deviation from such specified attributes has been thus established [be otherwise]?
"Śaṅkara is my very self"—thinking thus, he says:
"In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged, because its nature is unobscured, there is no obstruction anywhere. (2)

Of this aforementioned reality, there is no restriction—no limitation, no cause for designating it as "this" or "that," nor any attribute of an object of knowledge—in any place, time, form, or particular state; why? Because its nature is unobscured.
Because of its state of being such— that is, because its nature is that whose form is not covered or obscured by the impurity consisting of the conceit of birth and so forth. Of that [nature].

To establish the proof of its being unobstructed, he provides the qualification: "that in which all this effect resides and from which it has emerged. The word "this" refers to everything that exists as an object of cognition; "all" refers to whatever has been conceptualized in whatever philosophical system (*darśana*) and in whatever manner—that entirety of effects, whose existence is dependent upon an agent—resides in "that," meaning in which [Brahman].

It abides as one, established through its nature as the knower and the agent, serving as the universal substratum for the entire multitude of objects to be contained within it; for it is by virtue of this that every object existing within it becomes manifest, having attained its established form through various manifestations such as earth and so forth, or jars, cloths, cows, and so on.

The meaning is "the attainment of existence in its own nature. Now, one might object: "Just as substances such as jars and cloths, being situated within the light of the sun and other sources, attain existence by being manifested in their respective forms, so too is it said that all this effect attains existence by abiding therein [in the cause];
or is it by some other manner? To this he says: "And from which it has emerged."
Because it has emerged, arisen, from a single cause that is its sole agent, having excluded other causes such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter), this is the meaning here: that which...

The *padārtha* (the ultimate reality) is the foundation (*ādhāra*) because it exists as the sole illuminator of the multitude of principles— which, having attained the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), constitute the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and are categorized in various ways within the scriptures—

and it is the source (*prabhava*) or cause because it acts as the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, it is so because it cannot itself be touched by the quality of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*).
That which is not an object for other subjects consisting of *māyā*, whose majesty is undivided, and whose sole nature is pure, stainless consciousness—

that alone is intended here by the term "one's own essential nature" (*svasvabhāva*), and not the multitude of living beings who fall within the category of effects, whose selves are contracted by the conceit of being limited by genus and so forth, and whose consciousness of their own sovereignty has been eclipsed by the power of *māyā*.

"Own-nature" (*svarūpa*) means one's own essential being (*svabhāva*). Thus it was rightly said that "Ātman alone is Śaṅkara. Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti* raises an objection: "But how can there be a designation of the transmigrating soul, who is nothing other than his own essential being, as being Śiva? [He answers this by stating: "That wherein this world resides and from which it has arisen..."
This has been explained by the author while commenting [on the verse beginning] "p.
18)," [referring to] its state during saṃsāra.

Thus, the mode of being (*vṛtti*) should be understood as follows: for transmigrating beings, there is a state consisting of the illusory identification with birth and so forth manifested by that Māyā; yet even in that state, there is no real cessation of their own true nature (*svasvabhāva*). || 2 ||

Now, as for this category of reality called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) thus established— is it to be accepted as "yes" based solely on the authority of scripture, or can it be brought within the range of comprehension by means of the two well-founded methods of logical proof and empirical perception?
In order to introduce the logical justification (*upapatti*) which he will set forth in a subsequent verse for the purpose of cutting through doubt,

this is first stated: at the moment of reflecting upon one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*) by means of supreme wisdom (*prajñā*) that has attained firm establishment in the reality of the meaning to be expounded throughout the entire treatise.
But now, by the power of Māyā— which manifests as the darkness of the great delusion of duality and whose nature is perishing as it dispels the mass of mist touched by the rays of the sun—

For all subjects who are possessed [by this state], there arises—due to a fall, as it were, from their ultimate nature as the knower—the cognition "I" with respect to the body and so forth, which are merely objects of knowledge; this is the root of the knot of duality, which is extremely difficult to untie.
Therefore, for the sake of separating that essential nature, consisting of the "I-cognition," from those bodies and other such things...
Introducing the proof of his own experience as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the apprehension of the total absence of cessation— which was just asserted— he says:
"Even though there is a distinction between the waking state and so forth, it (consciousness) proceeds undifferentiated."
It does not at all turn away from its own nature as the perceiver. || 3 ||

Therefore, there is no cessation anywhere of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it does not turn away from its own innate, unconditioned intrinsic nature—that is, from its essential form (*svarūpa*)—nor does it become otherwise, nor does it fall away; such is the connection [of the words]. From what kind of intrinsic nature? From that which is the perceiver (*upalabdhṛ*), the apprehender (*upalambhaka*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), and the experiencer (*anubhavitṛ*); this is the meaning.

And when does it not cease? Even as the distinction consisting of waking and so forth unfolds— that is, as the differentiation, the exclusion, the mutual distinctness of the states spreads forth— even then [it does not cease].

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term *vijṛmbhamāṇe*, the states of dreaming and deep sleep (*suṣupta*) are included; the states of memory and so on are subsumed under dreaming because they share a similar nature, while the states of intoxication, fainting, and the like are subsumed under deep sleep. Among these, the state known as "waking" (*jāgrat*) is well-established in the scriptures as that state in which one perceives sounds and other objects through the sense organs, such as the ear.

The person, having his power extended, vibrates while grasping the objects of the senses. Dream is that state of sleep in which, though exhausted by its own activity and having ceased the wandering of the ears and other senses, he still perceives objects through the mind alone. Deep sleep is the state of pleasant slumber characterized by profound drowsiness, wherein even the activity of the mind has ceased.

When [the mind] has subsided, there is no perception of an object distinct [from itself] at that time. The state of memory consists in the non-forgetting of an experienced object; it is like a dream because of the similarity in the way the mind grasps the object. Intoxication (*mada*) is a transformation consisting in the loss of the functions of the mind and the senses, produced by excessive drinking. Fainting (*mūrchā*)...

The nature of which consists of delusion produced by the consumption of poison, alcohol, and so forth— because of the similarity in the absence of the apprehension of such objects of knowledge (*vedya*) and other such factors— whatever other states may possibly exist that are equal to deep sleep (*suṣupta*), they are all subsumed within these very [three] states. This being the cause...

Even when a distinction arises, this [perceiver] does not deviate from its own nature as a perceiver. If this perceiver were merely of the nature of the states themselves, then like those states, it too would undergo differentiation. However, while that differentiation spreads among them, this [perceiver] does not deviate from its own nature, which is distinct from the states. This is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also). How is this so?

We proceed as follows: even while being the substratum (*avasthātṛ*), he does not deviate from his single nature (*svabhāva*) even as the states (*avasthā*)—which possess distinct forms—unfold. Regarding this, he provides a qualifying attribute containing the reason (*hetugarbha*): "In what manner does he proceed? [The answer is: in that which is non-different from them; that is, non-different, having a single form.

In that [state] which is characterized by the mere fact of being a non-distinct perceiver, wherein one's own nature is experienced as all-pervasive; for even amidst a difference of states, there is no difference in the substratum whose characteristic is that of the perceiver.

Thus, in this matter, everyone’s own experience is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the states such as waking and so forth are experienced by oneself as being bound together by a single thread of a unifying subject, in the form: "I, who slept, am now awake."

They pervade. And no other state beyond these is possible for transmigrating beings, even though they are infinite in number. Therefore, just as in a single body that which is perceived as distinct from the states is one and all-pervading, so too in all bodies he alone is established as the one all-pervading self, despite the difference between bodies.

Because there is no other defining characteristic apart from the mere state of being the perceiver; and because the notion "I," which occurs as distinct for each individual, is illusory and not real. It is precisely for the purpose of setting that notion aside that this treatise is commenced. Furthermore, even that [notion] does not deviate from the single, unique self-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) which is the mere state of being the perceiver. Thus, Śaṅkara is indeed one's own essential nature.
Thus has it been correctly established for those awakened ones who do not deny their own experience. By means of these very states,
it should be understood that its non-difference from the states well-known in the Yoga scriptures— such as waking and the rest— is also demonstrated.

23) Even among those [states], because it abides as the perceiver and as the pervasive [principle], they are briefly defined. Among them, the mere sudden engagement of the mind toward the object of meditation is well known in some places as the state of waking (*jāgarāvasthā*) or *dhāraṇā*.

In that very state, the continuous flow of a uniform mental impression (*pratyaya*) through the avoidance of dissimilar impressions is what they call the meditative state of dreaming (*svapnāvasthā-dhyāna*). Through the gradual intensification of one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*), the mind reaches a state where it consists solely of the subtle appearance of the object of meditation, unmixed with other impressions; this is the state of dreamless sleep (*savedya-suṣuptāvasthā*).

That which they describe as a specific state of cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration—characterized by the accompaniment of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*)—is that which follows after bliss and the sense of self alone. But the other [concentration], preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*), wherein only residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain, is different [from the cognitive]. (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.17)

Thus defined, asamprajñāta-samādhi is that deep sleep which is beyond all objects of cognition. And throughout all these states, the existence of the one pervasive essential nature, whose form is the experiencer, remains ever established.

For, as long as concentration (*samādhi*) possesses an object (*sālambana*), the existence of the knower—the perceiver—is clearly evident due to the presence of a distinct object of knowledge, just as in the worldly state. However, where there is an absence of form due to being objectless (*nirālambana*), at that very time there is merely the non-perception of the object; it is not, however, an absence of the knower’s nature as a knower, as in deep sleep and similar states. Therefore...

That state of the one who has emerged [from the body], having become known through the fact of being remembered, indeed manifests the existence of the all-pervasive [Self]. As for those, however, who—deluded by the mere absence of the capacity to perceive what is perceivable—regard the perceiving Self itself as non-existent, he will awaken them later on. All of this...
The author of the commentary (Vṛttikṛt),

having indicated by means of the passage beginning with "Even when distinctions such as waking and so forth are occurring, its essential nature is not obscured," has established this through the analogy of the potency of poison. || 3 ||
Now, in specific states such as waking and so forth, this [self] does not deviate from its own nature— that is, from the form of the perceiver— by its very essence (p. 25).

As for what was established—that because the cognizer, which is knowledge, exists in the form of self-experience, it persists as a single nature—how can that be so? For in those various states, such cognitions arise for the very experiencer, namely: "I am a human," "I am a Brahmin," "I am Devadatta."
"I am young," "I am old," "I am thin," "I am fat"—these and others have the body as their basis;

"I am happy," "I am miserable"—these and others have the intellect (*buddhi*) as their basis; "I am hungry," "I am thirsty"—this is cognizable through the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one who has awakened from states such as deep sleep, and has the void (*śūnya*) as its basis.

It arises. All these things, such as the body and so forth, are impermanent; therefore, the notion of "I" which has them as its object is also necessarily impermanent. To the question, "How then can it be said that this [notion] does not cease from the nature of the perceiver (the meaning being: 'from the nature of the subject who perceives')?", he says:
The cognitions "I am happy," "I am miserable," and "I am attached," and so forth,
clearly persist elsewhere [in the subject] as that which is continuous through states such as happiness. (4)

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: those cognitions such as "I am happy" and so forth exist elsewhere; therefore, he does not turn away from that single nature. Because they are internal, the primary cognitions having the intellect (*buddhi*) as their object are indicated here. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), however, the cognitions having the body and so forth as their objects are subsumed. And these were previously...

Thus, all these cognitions exist elsewhere—in one who perceives pleasure and the other states—distinct from those previously described states such as pleasure itself; they abide there in unity, their mutual distinctions dissolved like rivers in the ocean, meaning they attain identity with that [perceiver]. And this is clear.

Because it is to be known through one's own direct experience, it is indeed perfectly manifest. Therefore, consciousness alone—manifesting as the "I" in the form of the perceiver—is the ultimate reality;
yet, due to the absence of such a reflective awareness of its true nature caused by the power of *māyā*, it appears as the knower of impermanent objects such as pleasure and the like.
(27) By the statement "I am happy" and "I am miserable," and so forth, consciousness (*saṃvit*)— having attained grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with states such as cognition—

is indicated by the plural form "consciousnesses" (*saṃvidaḥ*). If, however, [it were argued that consciousness appears as many] due to its connection with objects of experience such as pleasure, just like pleasure itself...

If even cognitions were, in the ultimate sense, multiple in nature like the notion of "I," then there could be no synthesis such as memory or recognition; and in the absence of that synthesis, the cessation of all worldly transaction would follow, which is not desired. Therefore, he provides a qualification for the object indicated by the word "elsewhere": "these."

In what manner do cognitions exist elsewhere? [They exist] within all states such as pleasure and so forth—specific conditions consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—which are impermanent because they possess the nature of arising and perishing, and which, by virtue of their common quality of being objects of cognition, function similarly to objects such as sound and the like; [they exist] within that which has the nature of being perceived as "I."

While abiding as a pervasive unity in a single form, two objects flash forth when such cognitions as "I am happy" or "I am suffering" arise; one of these is the self consisting of happiness and so forth.

The object of cognition (*vedyarūpa*)—because it is an object of cognition, like a jar or other objects—is understood to be impermanent and manifold. Another is the subject of cognition (*vedakarūpa*), which is established by all cognizers as pervading prior and subsequent states; it is eternal, being the agent of synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), which is the cause of all worldly transactions.

Because its nature consists solely of the perceiver, it shines forth as one alone. Thus, just as this [consciousness] remains one with an undivided essential characteristic even while diversity spreads through causes such as waking and so forth,
so too does it remain one even while diversity proceeds through the cause of the continuum of cognitions such as pleasure and so forth occurring within the states of waking and the rest.

Since it possesses an undifferentiated intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) and is truly one, even here [in this life] states such as "I who was happy have now become unhappy" or "am impassioned" are perceived as being bound together by a single unifying subject (*anusaṃdhātṛ*). Therefore,
[there is no difference whatsoever] even with respect to all the various particular states occurring within the mental continua of infinite sentient beings.
The alteration of the nature of that which consists merely of the non-arisen perceiver is self-established, because its form is eternally unobscured.
"Śaṃkara is indeed the ultimate reality, the very self-nature that is unceasing everywhere. Having explained this with the words "And he is indeed woven through all states," and so forth—
That is remembered as the supreme intrinsic nature.
Thus it was established as the final conclusion by the author of the Vṛtti. || 4 ||

Having thus established that it is logical to designate one's own essential nature as Śiva, he now states its definition in brief and says, in order to demonstrate its ultimate reality: "Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the object of perception nor the perceiver, and even no state of delusion—that exists in the ultimate sense. (5)

That entity, characterized by the qualifiers to be mentioned hereafter and denoted by the term "own-nature" (*svasvabhāva*), exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) and in reality (*tattvataḥ*);

everything other than that is unreal and non-existent—this is the meaning. What is it? It is that wherein there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither the grasped (*grāhya*) nor the grasper (*grāhaka*), and even no state of delusion (*mūḍhabhāva*). By this...

By negating its nature as pleasure and so forth, its state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is negated. For there are two kinds of objects of cognition: external and internal. Among these, the internal consists of pleasure and so forth.
Because it is to be known by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), that [state] does not exist there, since its nature has been established as being solely that of a distinct knower.

External objects of knowledge, such as sound and so forth, are designated by the term "the graspable" (*grāhya*); for they are apprehended by the external senses, such as the ear, and are then experienced by the internal organ as consisting of pleasure and so on—that too does not exist there. Indeed, its form is not [perceived].

It becomes an object of perception by virtue of having sound and other sense-objects as its nature. Furthermore, the "grasper" intended here is the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛ*), and not the ultimate subject whose nature is that of pure consciousness (*upalabdhṛ-mātra-svarūpa*), since the latter is established as being eternally existent. Thus, there is no illusory grasper—composed of the egoity of the body and so forth—even where such a thing might otherwise appear.

If, however, the reading is *grāhakam*, they explain it as "the sense organ (*indriya*)," but that too does not exist [in this state]. Thus, that reality which is of the nature of a mere grasper, distinct from the essential nature of the grasped and the act of grasping—that exists.
But surely, if this were so, this would be nothing other than a state of delusion?
Thus it has been established that in that [state], there is an absence of the nature of pleasure and so forth. To refute this, he says:
"And even the state of being deluded does not exist"—the state of one who is deluded is *mūḍhatva*.

The absence of the capacity for being an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and for knowing (*vedana*)—that too does not exist where it is not found; because even in that state, when one reflects back, "I was deluded," its status as an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) remains established, though there is simply a non-perception at that time. And since the quality of being an object of knowledge exists, how could the state of delusion [not exist]?

If it were the case that [the object] consisted of a reality whose nature is the single essence of being a cognizer, then even the state of being deluded would not exist therein; for, by negating the nature of all cognizable objects that fall within the scope of its apprehension, it would be established that it is a mere non-existence. To refute that, he says: "That exists in the ultimate sense"—that which...

Thus explained by way of its specific characteristics, that reality exists eternally in the ultimate sense, because its intrinsic nature is defined as the unceasing characteristic of the mere perceiver. On the other hand, that which consists of pleasure and so forth has its essence obtained through mere conceptual construction; it is momentary, perishable, and always an object of cognition, since its sole nature is that of being perceived.
It is far removed from the Self (p. 32). Therefore, whatever exists within the sphere of the knowable is all unreal because of its impermanence. But that which...

The meaning is that he alone, the knower, is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). This has been explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) in the passage beginning with "this is his nature" (*tat idaṃ tasya cāyaṃ svabhāvaḥ*). || 5 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate that this very Śiva— the Self who exists in the ultimate sense— is the most worthy of being accepted by first establishing His independent power to bring about all things,
he speaks this pair of verses: "Now, of this very Śiva, the Self who exists in the ultimate sense..."
In order to demonstrate that [the Lord] is the most worthy of being accepted by first establishing His independent power to accomplish all things,
he speaks this pair of verses:
"Since this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts as if undeluded..."
Together with the intermediate wheel, [it performs] the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
One should diligently and with reverence examine that reality through such effort,
for its independence is everywhere natural and uncreated.

That reality, known as one's own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*), which exists as ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*), [should be realized] through effort—that is, through intense and constant exertion that is never abandoned—and through devotion, meaning with an excess of faith.

In all states of experience, that which is to be examined should be made manifest as the Self through the reflective awareness of the nature of the cognizer, by means of sequentially dividing the two groups characterized as the object and the subject according to the instructions to be described hereafter;
for this very independence of His is what is now being introduced in this exposition.

It consists in the capacity to perform all actions solely by one's own will; it is innate and natural, existing everywhere— in every body or in every particular state— even for one who remains [in that state], and it does not depend on other causes such as material or auxiliary factors,
since even for transmigrating beings, the accomplishment of all worldly transactions occurs solely through the majesty of that very sovereignty.

However, due to the power of illusion and delusion, and because of the absence of any inquiry into the true nature of reality, every transmigrating being acts as if dependent, since in all their activities they accomplish all ends by depending on external causes. Therefore, that reality must be investigated in order to attain innate sovereignty, and not otherwise.

It has been taught that because pleasure, pain, and delusion, as well as the forms of the grasped and the grasper, are negated, it must be understood as being without substantial reality; now [this will be further explained]. (p. 34)

In order to establish the independence indicated by the word "this" (*iyam*), the qualification characterized by the relative pronoun *yat* is explained. What is that reality (*tattva*) to be examined? It is that from which this group of instruments—the external instruments such as the ears and so forth, and the internal ones such as the mind and so forth—[proceeds].

The group of the senses—the aggregate of the thirteen instruments—attains activity (*pravṛtti*), stability (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*). Activity is the state of emerging toward the object desired to be grasped; stability is the state of resting upon the object already grasped; and withdrawal is the abandonment of external objects due to having accomplished one's purpose.

The group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*)—which is generally known as being deluded and characterized by insentience alone—attains and reaches these states of cessation and dissolution. How does it attain them?
[It does so] through the power of contact with that which is the external and internal wheel of the senses, capable of the conscious activities such as engagement (*pravṛtti*).
When that reality has been made manifest as the Self, it possesses the sovereignty to bestow consciousness upon the senses, and thereby attains sovereignty over all objects.
Therefore, it must indeed be examined by what means, while still in the state of practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), autonomy (*svātantrya*) is manifested such that play (*krīḍā*)—
such as entering another's body (*paraśarīrāveśa*) and so forth— is rendered possible. This [autonomy] is not of the nature of pleasure and the like when it does not exist.
This and more has been explained separately in the Vṛtti by such passages as "Therefore, that reality must be examined with effort," and so forth. (7)

Now, why is this being said? Is there some such reality to be examined, by virtue of which the sense organs become conscious, such that worldly convention is established in this way— that every conscious cognizer,
through connection with merit and demerit, becomes joined with the quality called desire regarding what is to be avoided or what is to be accepted?

Having become attentive toward an object, he impels the group of insentient instruments by means of that very quality called "will" (*icchā*) toward the acceptance or rejection of various objects; and being thus impelled, the instrument—though itself insentient like an axe or similar tool—performs its own function.
How, then, can it be said that [the Self acts] "as if not deluded," since [the actual cause] is that which possesses the causal nature?

It has been explained that [the self] "attains activity and so forth"— anticipating the objection: "Is it not the case that it becomes capable of accomplishing the mental operations of activity and so forth solely by the power of contact with [the mind]?"— it is stated as follows.

In order to clarify how this group of instruments becomes conscious through the demonstration of the worldly activity of the transmigrating person (saṃsāri-puruṣa), he says: "For this [group] does not function as an impeller by means of a desire-impulse;
rather, through contact with the power of the Self (ātman), the person becomes equal to it. (8)

Indeed, it is not the case that for one impelled by desire, the desire itself is the "impeller"—that is, the instrument such as a goad by which one is driven. Rather, it is this transmigrating person, the cognizer (*pramātā*), who exists and persists as the impeller toward the group of sense organs by acting as their motivator. Just as someone like Devadatta, by means of an instrument such as his hand, drives a dull object like a goad.
This internal person does not impel the insentient collection of instruments toward their respective objects by means of his own will;
rather, it is through the touch of the power of the Self—that is, of the supreme subject, the all-doing Lord himself—[that they act].

Whatever is the power and capacity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—the ability to bring about all things independently of other causes—by contact with that, by association with that, one becomes equal to it; that is, one becomes identical with that "other" agent denoted by the word "Self. The intended meaning here is as follows: in whatever [case]...
Abiding in its own essential nature, the Supreme Lord— designated by the term "Self"—

is independent in bringing about the emergence, maintenance, and withdrawal of this universe as He desires; likewise, abiding in that very state, this transmigrating person is also independent in causing the group of instruments to engage with their respective objects and so forth, and for that reason, he is equal to Him.
Thus it has been said. Therefore, just as the Lord, by means of His two all-pervading powers called knowledge and action,
brings about the activity of the universe and so forth, knowing and acting upon everything, so too the individual soul (puruṣa),
through the mere touch of that power, having acquired the capacity for knowledge and agency, [acts] by virtue of Māyā through [powers] whose objects are restricted.
Through the powers of knowledge and action, which have issued forth as the internal and external groups of instruments, he knows and acts upon his own objects; thus his equality with them is stated,
yet he does not impel the instruments by means of the impulse of will.
This and more has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). || 8 ||

But surely, by setting the group of instruments into operation within its own function, the person attains sovereignty just like the Lord due to occupying the station of the Lord; thus, would it not be established that there is indeed no difference between those two—the Lord and the person? How then is the person's equality with the Lord established on the basis of their difference in that state? [End of citation]
When the agitation of one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desirous of performing duties,
dissolves away, then the supreme state is attained.

It is true that there is non-difference between these two in that state; however, this person, due to the cause of impurity— namely, his own innate defilement consisting of passion and the like rooted in the identification of the self with the body and so forth—

is desirous and greedy for a mere fragment of momentary pleasure, and by means of that very [defilement], he engages in the activities to be performed which serve as the causes for obtaining the objects that are the means to that [pleasure].
When one who is incapable and destitute of power— because, even though desiring it, he does not obtain what is desired— finds himself in such a state (p.

When the agitation— the illusory affliction consisting of the notion of "I" which takes as its support the body and so forth— is dissolved at the proper time through contact with the light of the sun that is the natural notion of "I," which has transcended artificial supports,
it would melt away and perish like a mass of frost; then there would be the supreme, unsurpassed state or station.

"It should manifest through its true being" means that non-duality—the identity between the two consciousnesses, the supreme (*parā*) and the inferior (*aparā*), denoted by the terms "Self" (*ātman*) and "Person" (*puruṣa*)—should be proclaimed as something perceived precisely in that state.
This very point—that "this is established in its own essential nature"—is what is set forth by this verse. Let it be demonstrated.

In other philosophical systems, this impurity of the person is described in various ways; however, in this system, it is precisely this much: namely, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya). For all conceptions of being a transmigrating being are based solely upon that [notion].
When that very notion has dissolved, there arises the supreme state, characterized by the manifestation of one's own true nature.
40) Regarding "purity": as it has been said—when the island of the notion of a body has collapsed upon birth, and [the self] has reached oneness in the stainless ocean of consciousness.
Without ever withdrawing the aggregate of your senses, you, the inner self of the universe, eternally shine as the one.
Likewise, even though the self is not independent, no one is able to employ the universe at will, as if it were their own hands and other limbs;
for like children or kings, they lack awareness of their own power, whereas when you reside within them, everyone possesses all power.
Thus, this has already been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the passage beginning with "that and his" (*sa cāsya*), and so forth. || 9 ||

Now, it may be objected: since the Self alone— characterized by a state of supreme tranquility like an ocean undisturbed by wind, wherein the agitation consisting of the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth has dissolved— is what is designated by the term "Supreme Abode," how could the person, through contact with its power, incur a quality as different from it as that, namely agitation itself,
by being joined with which he causes the group of senses to engage in activity and the like?
Thinking "I act" and "I know"—
thus apprehending its own object— it becomes truly agitated.
To shatter the confusion of mind in those who do not know the Self, he said:
"Then his innate nature, characterized by knowledge and agency, exists;
for by means of it, he knows and performs everything he desires. (10)

Then, at that time characterized by the complete cessation of the aforementioned agitation, there remains indeed for this self an innate, spontaneously accomplished, and eternally inseparable attribute—namely, the quality (guṇa) defined as the nature of knowing and agency; this is the implied meaning.
For, from that non-deviating quality acting as the cause, everything desired [is attained] in its capacity as an object of knowledge.

When that person desires to obtain an object as an effect, then— and not at any other time— in that state characterized by the union consisting of the relationship with the true nature [of reality], he both knows and acts. What has been said?

[It] becomes [so]; that which is called "knowing-ness" (jñatva) or "apprehending-ness" (upalabdhṛtva) is a quality not distinct from this self, and it [belongs to] that which is to be determined as "this" (idantā).

Because the object (*vastu*) is twofold—by virtue of being that which is to be known (*jñeya*) and that which is to be produced (*kārya*)—it is figuratively designated as having a dual nature. In reality, however, it is said to be one alone, consisting of the Lord’s self-reflective awareness (*svabhāvapratyavamarśa*), and it is proclaimed by the term "action" (*kriyā*) because its very essence is the exertion of that [awareness] alone. And such a quality belongs to Him, untouched by the affliction of the perception of objectivity (*vedyatva*).

For one who abides in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by being the sole knower (*vedakaika*), there unfolds omniscience and universal agency. On the other hand, that knowledge and agency which— due to the absence of such reflective awareness of one's own nature— is based on the notion of a knower with respect to the body and so forth, which are merely objects of cognition (*vedya*), is artificial and limited in scope.

Therefore, the nature of the Self consists precisely in its essential attributes characterized by consciousness and agency, and not in a state of agitation. And a transmigrating person, touching such power of the Self and being endowed with consciousness and agency regarding his own objects through the activation of the group of instruments and so forth, becomes equal to it.
Thus, that which was stated is indeed established;
this very point the author of the commentary (vṛttikṛt) explains with the words beginning, "In that time characterized by the dissolution of agitation," and so forth. || 10 ||
43) Having thus established the nature of the self through reasoning, he says the following to demonstrate the fruit of its realization:
"Beholding that intrinsic nature as the presiding subject..."
How could such a crooked path belong to one who remains as if smiling? || 11 ||
The word "that" (*tam*) refers back by means of a pronoun to the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) set forth in the ten preceding verses.

Because that very Self, characterized in such a way, exists as the presiding principle (*adhiṣṭhātṛbhāva*) within all bodies, at all times, in all states, and everywhere—pervading everything merely as the experiencer—it has nothing else to preside over. Thus, it is "not to be presided over by another" (*ananyādhiṣṭheya*).

Beholding [reality] in the form "I alone am the independent Supreme Lord, the presiding authority"— seeing thus through the aforementioned perspective of logical reasoning (*upapatti-dṛś*) and the perspective of the instruction on realization (*upalabdhy-upadeśa-dṛś*) which will be described hereafter— one recognizes [one's own nature] and, as it were, smiles at the recognition of the true self as the supreme subject, which had previously been forgotten.

For one who, while contemplating how the nature of the illusory subject (māyīyapramātṛ), though unreal, manifests in this way, remains as if struck with wonder and experiences a state free from all disturbance—it is for such a person [that this is taught]. (p.

For the yogi, this well-known "evil path" (kusṛti)—which has as its sole root the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth—is a contemptible and censurable course (saraṇa) consisting of wandering through various other wombs due to the conjunction with the dualities of birth, old age, death, and so on; for what reason? Because it is of the nature of agitation (kṣobha) as previously explained.

The meaning is that because of the absence of impurity, which serves as the cause [for movement], there is no going at all for one who is seated, just like the movement of a sword [in the hand]. And this has been explained by the author of the Vṛtti with the words: "Since this Self is indeed all-pervasive," and so forth. || 11 ||

Now, in order to awaken those who think that because the reality of the Self— whose nature is devoid of all knowable attributes— is taught as something to be attained, it must therefore be taught as a mere non-existence, he says:
Non-existence cannot be brought into being, nor is there any lack of delusion regarding it;
for, through the touch of diligent application, there arises the certainty that "it existed. (12)

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the emptiness of entities; it does not become, that is, it does not go toward, the state of being an object of focus within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because existence and the cultivation of non-existence are mutually contradictory. Existence...
For only an entity capable of being an object of consciousness is fit to become an objective support (*ālambana*) by way of being meditated upon, and not "nothingness.
As it has been taught in a certain place:
"One should cultivate non-existence until one attains identification with it."

Thus it is said. Let it be that this state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which consists in the cessation of the conceptual constructions of the meditator, the act of meditation, and the object of meditation, is what those who have forgotten their true self consider to be "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Yet, in that particular state, there exists no "unconfusedness"—that is, no absence of delusion—because, upon contact with application [of effort], at the moment of emergence from that state, [delusion arises].

Through contact— that is, through the connection— with an application of mind directed toward the contemplation of such an interval between states, and with an expression arising at that very moment, there would arise a certainty (*niścaya*) or a determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "that interval has been" or "has passed.
What is meant?— the yogin, having attained firm establishment in the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*), from that...
If, having emerged [from meditative absorption], he were not to reconnect with that state, how could he have the conviction, "I have attained stability"?
And in the absence of that [conviction], there would be no distinction between meditative absorption and emergence.
There is no apprehension of difference [between the states]. Therefore, one necessarily remembers: "At that time, I experienced such a state.

And because it is remembered as something past, it is non-eternal—like pleasure and so forth—and cannot be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self, since that which is of the nature of consciousness exists eternally as the experiencer.
The state of being remembered by another rememberer is not possible; this has been explained in the *Vṛtti* with the passage beginning, "But non-existence is not to be cultivated," and so forth. 12.
To clarify this, he says:
"Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep;
however, that reality does not attain such a state of being remembered. (13)

Therefore, because it is designated as having been "that" in the past, that entity known as the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāvasamādhi*) should be understood as artificial, since it is produced by conceptual construction due to its association with the states of existence and non-existence.

It must always be understood as impermanent; there is not even a fraction of time in which such a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) remains as something permanent. How can it be known as artificial? It is similar to that [state] which has consciousness as its locus. What is meant by this? Just as the worldly...

The state of deep sleep, because its nature consists of dense delusion, is as if non-existent since the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, though existing, is not apprehended at that time; yet, being brought within the scope of subsequent reflection upon awakening, it is impermanent because it is remembered as something past. Similarly, the state of absorption into non-existence is also impermanent at the time of emergence.

This is because they share the commonality of being remembered as having been real. By this, it is established that all such meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) are included within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*); however, that reality—the entity characterized by its own essential nature—is not here taught as something to be primarily adopted in the manner described.

It attains the state of being remembered, for because it is eternally risen, it is always indeed present. Thus, even for one who has attained the stage of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the contemplation of its non-existence (p. 48), [it remains so].
This and more has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). || 13 ||

Now, although that reality (tattva) is always manifest because it is eternally emergent, it is nonetheless the cause of bondage because it is not recognized as such. Therefore, by means of the received instruction, one should— throughout all states— focus on the aspect of the knower (*vedaka*), which is intent upon discerning the entire manifold universe (*viśvaprapañca*) as it is subsumed within the two-fold reality of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).
"One must make it one's own by reflecting upon it as being transcendent even from the nature of all objects of knowledge, [thinking] 'I am'.
To teach this, he says the following in order to demonstrate that the duality of that reality, manifested through the power of its own *māyā*:
"And here, there is a pair of states designated as 'objectivity' and 'agency'."
In that regard, the state of being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable.
In this case, within this supreme reality called the Self (ātman) which has been explained here, two states (avasthā-dvayam) are possible.

By this, although the objects to be abandoned and those to be adopted are infinite—due to the distinctions of reality (*tattva*) and so forth established through the systems of various philosophical schools—they are nonetheless subsumed under a duality alone because of their connection with the two characteristics.
The meaning is that, despite the infinity of the world's manifoldness, there are only two principles. However, only the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

The Self, by means of the power of its own sovereignty which is incomparable, unobstructed, and free from substrate, sports while manifesting itself as a duality; this is what is intended to be demonstrated by the use of the term "states" (*avasthā*). The meaning is that that single reality alone exists in a state of duality. What kind of pair of states is it? [The answer follows:]...

The state "I" is one, which is independent; the second, however, is its opposite, consisting of effects, being an object of enjoyment, knowable, insentient, and dependent. By the word "designated" (*śabdita*), it is established that there is only a difference in the names of these two and no real ontological distinction. Therefore, [the second] consists of effects.
p.

50) This state does not differ from the Self—the supreme cause—which is designated by the term "agent" because its nature consists solely of manifestation, and whose essence is light alone; for [the state] consists of the wheel of powers (śakticakra).

That this reality is the source of its own manifestation has already been established. In that state consisting of such a pair of conditions, the state of being an effect is perishable; the state in the form of an effect is subject to momentary dissolution. Whatever is determined as having the nature of an effect precisely because of its lack of awareness of the blossomed reality—all that [is perishable].
Due to its connection with arising and passing away, agency (*kartṛtva*) perishes at every moment;

however, the state of being the agent (*kartṛ-rūpa-avasthā*) is imperishable and eternal, because it possesses only the attribute of being the perceiver (*upalabdhṛtva-mātra-dharmaka*), which is found to pervade all states as eternally manifest. Thus, one should always regard this single entity—the agent, the knower, and the universal presiding controller—as the Self.
"For one who remains while maintaining continuity [of awareness], bondage is impossible"— this is the connection with the preceding verse.
This very thing constitutes the two states.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of such [passages]. || 14 ||

(51) Now, it has been stated that the reality which is the nature of the perceiver is imperishable; however, this is indeed untenable, because in states such as the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāvasamādhi*), there is an absence of the very form of the perceived. How, then, can its imperishability be maintained?
Only that effort which is directed toward an object is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed. (15)

When one is intent upon an object that is to be accomplished, fashioned, or known, and exerts an effort inclined toward its realization in that manner—that innate enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is agency (*kartṛtva*). That alone is the supreme cause, the motive for the operation;
because in that state the gross form of the effect is absent, it is as if lost, being unmanifest within the self.
It remains as if it has become subservient. When that effort has been dissolved at that very moment, the ignorant person—
one devoid of the realization of reality— conceives the thought, "I am destroyed," because such a cognition arises for one who defines the object by distinguishing it from the state of being.

If it is determined that this [self] exists as an agent even prior to [the act of cognition], then how could it be the object of negation, since it is already established? Thus, this follows: just as some Devadatta...
When someone staying at home is called by another, "O Devadatta!

and, wishing to deny his own existence, replies, "I am not here," by saying this he actually demonstrates, on the contrary, that "I am present," rather than his absence. Therefore, even in states such as the meditative absorption of non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*), [the self persists].
The notion of the self's non-existence arising merely from the cessation of the activity of the instruments due to the absence of an object to be accomplished is nothing but an error;
this has been explained in the *Vṛtti* regarding the capacity for accomplishing an effect.
By [the words] beginning with "thus," etc. || 15 ||
To further clarify this very point, he says:
"But that inward state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience—its disappearance could never occur, because nothing else is perceived. (16)

But furthermore, there is never, at any time or in any circumstance, a lapse— that is, a destruction of its own nature— of that supreme reality which exists in the ultimate sense, even during those infinitesimal moments of time characterized by meditative absorption and so forth.

It might be argued that [the subject] could exist; however, this is not tenable because no other entity distinct from that [subject], which is of the nature of an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and impermanent, is perceived—that is, there is an absence of experience.

Indeed, it cannot be said that "there is no object of knowledge" and "there is also no knower. For whose [subjectivity] would there be no cessation? It is that which is inward-turned, because of the absence of any external object of knowledge distinct from it, and which exists within.
That reality called the Self (ātman) is such a state in which the power of knowledge resides solely within its own nature;

it is the locus of the quality of omniscience, the unique substratum for that attribute or property consisting in the capacity to cognize the entire range of knowable objects. The intended meaning here is that the Self [is defined] by the distinction between knowledge and action.

That power which is twofold, when the activities of the internal and external organs have ceased during the state of the *puruṣa*, remains as nothing but the cognitive power directed solely toward its own self; therefore, it is called an "inward-turned state. Furthermore, the use of the word "face" (*mukha*) for power is observed, as in the *Pārameśvara*.
The mouth of Śivā is said here [to be this].

In such passages as these, there exists, at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*), the impossibility of such a state otherwise. Those yogins perceive that state—which consists merely in the delusion of not grasping external objects—as "non-existence" (*abhāva*); however, for one whose power of cognition is never interrupted, there is no destruction whatsoever of that state, because no object distinct from the Self is ever perceived.

For at that time, he experiences his very own nature—which, like the surface of the cloudless sky, is entirely distinct [from all else] and all-pervading—as being of the form of pure consciousness alone; yet, due to being under the sway of delusion, having forgotten and failed to reconnect with his own essential nature, he does not realize it as such. But when awakened, he realizes it just as...

He proceeds in such a manner; he will teach the means [thereto] further on. This has already been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the passage beginning with "he who is inward-turned, mounted upon the inner wheel," and so forth. || 16 ||

Thus ends the first outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), titled "The Instruction on the Establishment of Distinction," in the commentary on the *Spandakārikās* known as the *Vivṛti*, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāma. || 1 ||
(p. 55) Now,
as for what is called the perception of a distinct intrinsic nature:
The second is the outflow.

Thus, having established the reality of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth— exactly as promised— by means of reasoning proven through one’s own experience, it is now the occasion for the instruction on the means of perceiving that [Self].

Within the threefold worldly order, distinguished by the categories of the well-awakened, the awakened, and the unawakened, who indeed is the fit recipient for the instruction currently under discussion?
Thus, for the sake of establishing the scope [of the subject], he says:
"The perception of that [reality] is always inseparable from the three steps;
it is constant for one who is perfectly awakened, but for another, it occurs at its beginning and end. (1)

The realization, experience, and non-conceptual apprehension of that very Self, who has been described as the Supreme Lord, belongs eternally— at all times and in every state of experience— to one who is well-awakened, meaning perfectly awakened from the long and painful dream consisting of the ego-notion (*ahaṃpratyaya*) directed toward the body and other such objects.

For one who possesses right vision—who has accomplished what was to be accomplished and whose consciousness is not even slightly obscured by the great sleep of delusion—this is possible and appropriate.
Of what nature? It is constant, uninterrupted, and non-deviating from the three states throughout the three [times].

In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—across the various levels of consciousness—it is unchanging and non-contradictory because it is never overwhelmed by any condition; thus, its presence is immediate and uninterrupted. Consequently, for such a perfectly awakened one who has realized the supreme perfection characterized by mastery over his own self, there is simply no room for the subject matter of instruction here.
Because his task has been accomplished; and because for another— the second one who has awakened immediately following him—
the darkness of Māyā is being dispelled by the dawn-light of the descent of supreme grace (*para-śaktipāta*),
so that the clear eye of discernment (*viveka*) opens wide as the power of delusion (*moha*) wanes.
For those whose excellence of delusion and vigor does not manifest, regarding those three stages beginning with waking—
the stage that constitutes the beginning of them all, namely the waking state, and the two stages that constitute its end,
namely those called dreaming and deep sleep— in that [context], of that...
