57) There would be the apprehension of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*). According to the intention of the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*), the analysis (*vigraha*) of that initial and final term has been made as follows: since...

"In dream, deep sleep, and so forth"—by this, that word is explained. And here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of states such as memory and delusion, which are subsumed under the states of dreaming and deep sleep, is intended. Thus...

And the intention of this commentary is as follows: here, two types of instruction regarding the perception of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) have been introduced and are to be carried through to completion—one concerning the essential nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-svasvarūpa*) which is distinct from everything else, and the other concerning its power-circle (*tacchakticakra*) which constitutes the Self of the universe. Both forms of this instruction are present in this [work].

For one who is awakened, even in the two states of deep sleep and dreaming, the three stages [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] are generally of no further use, just as they are for one who is perfectly awakened;

this is because the realization of reality is achieved without effort simply through the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of consciousness residing in those two states, whereby the supreme reality is realized exactly as it has been explained.
This indeed occurs for him spontaneously (p.
58), as follows:
when, because all conceptualizations of objects of knowledge have dissolved away, he enters the exclusive state of deep sleep;
In the state of awakening, when one reflects upon the self,

then one personally realizes the reality of the self— which is free from all external taints, consisting solely of the repose in its own essential nature, and whose inherent character is that of a perpetually undeluded cognizer. And when, even in the absence of those various distinct causes of its own...

When one, being free from sleep, reflects upon one's own dream-state— which consists of the manifestation of a wheel of various conscious and unconscious entities appearing with extremely vivid clarity— then, by that very same analogy, through the power of awakening, one realizes the nature of the Supreme Lord, the ultimate cause.
One perceives that reality which consists in the state of being the agent of all things, independent of any cause other than one's own will alone.

However, for the unawakened person, even when this [reality] is offered with hundreds of efforts, it produces no internal contact, like water poured upon a gourd. Thus, in these two states, there may be perception for the awakened one—so it is said.
It is established that in the remaining two states called waking and the fourth (turya),
she does not belong to him— this is what is meant by implication. Therefore, in the waking state...

The supreme reality is obscured by the operations of the senses, which are preoccupied with grasping objects such as sound; furthermore, because it transcends the world, it is utterly unfamiliar even in the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) and is difficult to perceive on its own. Therefore, even one who is awakened to it requires instruction for its realization. As the author of the *Vṛtti* says:
"Waking and the fourth state are to be known through scripture alone"—
thus [it is said] regarding that all-pervading one whose nature is consciousness.
The author of the commentary explained this with these and other words. || 1 ||

Having thus established the scope of the instruction, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the differentiation within all four states—waking and the rest—of the Supreme Reality (pārameśvara-tattva), which exists in two modes: as being transcendent to everything and as possessing all forms.
"Endowed with the supreme Śakti, whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge..."
The All-pervasive One shines in two feet, but elsewhere He consists of pure consciousness.

The all-pervading Lord, the Sovereign whose form is pure consciousness, the Self, shines and manifests endowed with His own power and capacity— the supreme power that transcends all because of its most wondrous nature— within the two states known as waking and dreaming.
It shines forth. By what kind of power? By that which has the nature of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it consists of the internal and external circles of instruments (*karaṇacakra*), having the nature of grasping, or it is pure consciousness (*jñaptimātra*).

The "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) is the class of objects to be grasped, such as sound and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth, possessing infinite particularities. That very thing constitutes its form, and she is [the power] who possesses that form.

Thus it is by her. What is meant? The Supreme Lord himself, appearing in the form of various individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) through the power of his own *māyā*, manifests his own non-differentiated supreme power (*parā śakti*) in the form of knowledge and the object of knowledge, thereby bringing forth the worldly transactions of the waking and dreaming states; and this very thing—

The supremacy of this power is that, while not obscuring the manifestation of its own nature as sovereign majesty (*vaibhava*), it flashes forth as infinite forms consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge; whereas in the case of the differentiated,
there is merely the non-manifestation of non-duality.
In the darkness of *māyā*, where the delusion of the distinction between knower, knowledge, and the known has dissolved, there exists only the one ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*),
whose sole nature is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). It possesses a power characterized solely by the attribute of being the experiencer of such a self-nature.

This is accepted as the reality, since it is said elsewhere that [the Lord] is "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*). Therefore, other than—that is, apart from—the two aforementioned states, in the other two states designated as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the fourth (*turya*), the pervasive one shines as consisting of consciousness; He is the Self, the Lord, whose nature is that of the perceiver (*cetayitṛ*), having that [consciousness] alone as His material cause (*prakṛti*) in those two states.

The meaning is that, because there is no object of cognition distinct from the feet [of the Lord], the Lord alone shines forth, His power resting solely within His own partless Self. Now, one might object: since the waking and dreaming states consist of both knowledge and the knowable, while the deep sleep and the fourth (turya) states shine forth as consisting of consciousness alone, they are non-different; therefore, how can there be only two "feet"?
Regarding the phrase "the four quarters," it is said here that there is a distinction between the objects of the waking and dreaming states,

produced by the conceptualization of their stability or instability; therefore, those two [first] quarters exist because the creation imagined by the Lord appears with firmness during the waking state.

However, one proceeds [in this way] in a dream because of its lack of firmness; thus, this is the cause of distinction between these two states as they are conceptualized by the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
But in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), although the reality whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) exists, [it is not perceived].
Due to the power of delusion (*moha*), because of the absence of the wonder of the perceiver (*upalabdhṛ*) as "I," that very reality appears as if non-existent;

however, its perception as the Self through ultimate existence (*paramārthasattā*) occurs in the fourth state (*turyapada*). This is the distinction between deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the fourth state.
Therefore, there are exactly four states, designated by such names as Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya.
These [points] are also well-known in other treatises;
this has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of such statements as "it is of two forms through the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge. || 2 ||

Now, in order to further establish that it is only one who is awakened who is fit to be instructed according to the method just described, and to exclude those who are unawakened from that status, he speaks these three verses:
"The outpourings of the vibration of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth arise by depending upon the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda)."
Having attained their own self-nature, they would constantly be non-obstructive to the wise man. || 13 ||
But these [beings] of unawakened intellect, striving to conceal their own true state,
cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (4)
Therefore, one who is constantly diligent in discerning the reality of Spanda attains his own true nature even while awake, without delay.

Therefore, for the reason specified in the three verses of the present exposition, one who is "awake"—that is, truly enlightened—attains his own state, his own ultimate reality, in no long time, that is, in a very short period; he accepts it through perfect realization. By the word "only" (*eva*), the unenlightened person is excluded. In what manner does he attain it? [The answer follows:]...

This [treatise] is the most excellent means for the discernment— that is, the differentiation and separation— of that reality which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of what will be explained as having two modes by virtue of its nature consisting of both conventional universals and particulars; it is the form determined respectively as something to be adopted and something to be abandoned.

The innate property, which consists of the reflective awareness— “I am this very Self, the ultimate cause, the Truth; from Me everything originates, and into Me alone it dissolves”— is the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*).

Likewise, these particular fluctuations (*viśeṣaspanda*), which are to be utterly abandoned, give rise to the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) with respect to the body and other things that are not the Self; they have as their object the limited subjects born of *māyā* who are distinct from one another—
such streams of cognition consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*) as "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth— and they are the causes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

—Thus, constantly and without interruption in all circumstances, he is intent upon discernment; because his own strength is augmented by the realization of the means of proof through the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated, he is resolute with unimpeded enthusiasm. By this, being truly awakened and single-mindedly devoted to the cultivation of the means, he will in no long time...
It has been established that one perceives one’s own true nature (*svarūpa*) and no other. For what reason does he alone attain it and not another? To this he says:

"The outpourings of the vibration of the *guṇas*," and so forth. The connection is as follows: because for the knower (*jña*), the outpourings of the vibration of the *guṇas* and so forth would not be obstacles. Regarding these vibrations...

The outflows (*niḥṣyanda*) of the powers of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), such as knowledge and so forth, are distinct cognitions (*pratyaya*) that have issued forth as streams directed toward various objects.
The "outflows of vibration" (*spandaniṣyanda*) are the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; those for whom the primary [cause] is these qualities and so forth are the "qualities and so forth.

Being of the nature of pleasure and the rest, they consist of *sattva* and the other [qualities]. These "qualities and so forth" are the outflows of vibration—the various cognitions such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded. Of what form are they?
"Having obtained their self-nature by resorting to the universal vibration":

because they have properly resorted to—that is, taken refuge in and worshipped—the universal vibration, which is all-pervasive, in which infinite particular vibrations are latent within, and which is the manifestation of the power of the Supreme; "having obtained their self-nature" means that their self-nature has been attained or secured.

Those [phenomena] such as the fluctuations and outflows of qualities (guṇa) and so forth, which arise through various distinct forms as the attainment or emergence of one's own essential nature (ātman), are in fact nothing but the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda) for the Knower— one whose state as a subject (pramātṛbhāva) has arisen from the grace of the Supreme Lord through the cognition of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.

Because of the realization of the non-conceptual state established as the primary power of the Supreme Lord (p. 66), [the Self is distinguished] from those forms which appear mutually distinct due to the coloring of limiting adjuncts such as pleasure and so forth.

For one who has turned away from specific fluctuations and possesses self-confidence in their own power, who desires victory through constant effort in the practice of the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated, [the afflictions]— having their capacity to veil the nature [of consciousness] obstructed by the manifestation of their own strength— become non-opposing and free from adversaries.
They would become such that they are unable to destroy the zeal for the realization of the supreme reality; this is the intended meaning here:

whatever outpourings of vibration (*spanda*), consisting of the qualities (*guṇamaya*) and arising from the nature of pleasure and so forth, proceed as the continuous flow of cognitions for any given subject within the sphere of *māyā*, all of them are indeed one.

Relying upon the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), they each attain their respective individual selves; however, only the awakened one is a vessel for the wisdom that recognizes the arising of that [vibration]. Therefore, while he remains eternally diligent, these practitioners are unable to become [his equals]. As for those who...

(67) Because these [impurities] have an unstoppable flow for those whose intellects are unawakened, he says: "But those of unawakened intellect," and so forth. "Unawakened" means that their intellect (*dhīḥ*), i.e., their wisdom (*prajñā*), has not had its deep sleep of ignorance dispelled due to the absence of the supreme grace of the Lord.

Those [beings] for whom these aforementioned qualities and so forth are outflows resulting from the movement [of the mind]—they cause such persons to fall upon the path of saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross and hard to traverse because it is filled with hundreds of terrifying horrors; that is, they cause them to wander incessantly thereon along the continuous road of birth and so forth. Being of what nature [do they do this]? [They are those who...]

Stability arises from non-conceptual practice; it is a firm foundation. When its concealment—that is, its immediate veiling—is undertaken, they exert themselves because, due to the absence of awakening which serves as the counteragent, they have gained free rein and thus act in this manner. What is meant? Just as...
Certain [beings], such as kings and others,
because they exist in states of negligence and so forth, do not perceive their own capacity— such as that of an army— as being existent, even though it exists.

The opposing forces, looking for an opportunity and intent on displacing one from their own station, cast one into great calamity until they realize the existence of their own inherent power. Likewise, for the unawakened one who fails to recognize his own innate majesty— characterized by universal agency and so forth— which exists in the form of the universal vibration.

For one who perceives the very creation of the body and so forth— which is entirely dependent on all causal factors— as being the Self, these streams of cognitions, such as "I am happy," which consist of subordinate and primary qualities, gain their scope; by obstructing stability in the true Self,
they lead only to *saṃsāra* until the attainment of awakening— thus [it is said] by the awakened ones.

Thus, the objects of this instruction are not those who are unawakened. For even if the words of the instruction are somehow grasped by them, they do not find internal rest because their wisdom is weak regarding decisive realization.
As it has been said by someone:
Even when accepted as objects of knowledge, the words of instruction are unable to take root in the hearts of those with deluded minds;
for can showers from the clouds, though clinging closely and without interval, impart moisture to lotus leaves?
Thus [it is said]. In that regard, it is precisely in the waking state...

Thus, it should be understood that the passage from the commentary refers to the state of awakening (*prabuddhāvasthā*) in accordance with the present context. Alternatively, if the term "constantly striving" (*satatodyukta*) is taken to include the awakened one,

then the constantly striving awakened person, by means of the sequence of instruction to be described, [realizes] his own [nature] even during the waking state, in the very condition of worldly activity (*vyavahāradaśā*).
"He attains the state"—thus it should be explained. These three verses have been explained in detail according to their divisions in the *Vṛtti*;
therefore, he who performs [this] constantly, at all times—
By such passages as these;
likewise, by such passages as "of the vibration of the qualities (guṇaspanda) consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas," and so forth. Likewise...
By the passage beginning with "But those of very little understanding," etc., [the author explains]. (3) (4) (5)
Thus, having established that it is precisely for the awakened one that the states of waking and the fourth (turya) are to be taught,
[the author] speaks in order to instruct on the perception of the supreme reality, which is indeed merged within the intermediate state of waking common to all embodied beings:
"Whether extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting 'what shall I do?'"
Or, whatever step one may take while running, there the vibration is established.

70) Since vibration (*spanda*) exists in a twofold manner—being either established or unestablished according to the distinction between the universal and the particular—the connection [of the sentence] is as follows:
"the established vibration, which is to be accepted, is perceived in that state. That which...

Established as the ground for the designation of "movement," yet possessing an unshakable stability because it is not the object of specific, impermanent vibrations such as pleasure and the like, this primary movement is of the nature of a universal, supported by its own essence alone; it is a property of the Supreme Self (paramātman) in which the entire wheel of specific powers has completely subsided.
He should be observed in that very state which is being described right now:

in what state would he go while extremely enraged— overcome by an even more intense fury due to seeing an enemy, experiencing fresh and terrible calamities, and so forth— but rather, in the state of a transformation produced by that [fury] immediately upon its very first arising, before it has even fully developed.
Whatever stage one might reach or attain mentally, one should likewise go to that state with extreme joy; that is,
one should be thrilled by seeing a woman who has returned to life as if her breath had been restored,
and so forth— thrilled with a preeminent, supreme, and extraordinary degree of delight, overflowing with bliss, and thus filled with joy as soon as it arises.
Reflecting, "What shall I do so that I may reach that state?"—
that state which one might reach when attacked by an angry king or a powerful enemy, for the sake of countering it.

Failing to reach a decision on what ought to be done, and being utterly bewildered as to how to act—thinking "What shall I do? What means should I resort to here?"—one dwells in a state where the mental fluctuations lack any support; this is the meaning of "perceiving the vibration established therein. By these three modes [of practice],...

Suffering and happiness— such various other types as these should be understood to be included therein. Therefore, like one who is extremely enraged by a cause such as hearing of the destruction of an unsuspected beloved person, and so forth.

Just as one who is already overwhelmed by grief would go to that state where grief has merely begun to manifest even before the physical distortions such as the shedding of tears occur; and likewise, one who is extremely terrified by some cause— such as suddenly coming within the range of the jaws of an enraged black serpent or a tiger— would go to that very same state where fear has just arisen instantly.
Likewise, it has been taught that even when one reaches a place where disgust arises due to causes such as seeing objects that are utterly loathsome,
there too the vibration established in its own ground is perceived.
There exists a fourfold mass of suffering distinguished by anger, sorrow, fear, and disgust,
as indicated by the term "extremely enraged. Likewise,
due to causes such as the conceit of possessing one's own heroism, strength, and accomplishments, even a most difficult task—
Just as one who strives to bring about that very state free from conceptual construction might suddenly reach that state;

or likewise, one who is instantly overcome by extreme wonder through seeing objects such as those never before seen and supremely beautiful might suddenly reach that state; or similarly, one who reaches that state due to laughter arising from causes such as hypocrisy—even in those cases, [the same applies].

The perception of established vibration (*pratiṣṭhitaspandopalabdhi*) is thus taught. Furthermore, when one is overcome by doubt—due to the absence of certainty and determination regarding an object seen from a distance, etc., and being like one who is bewildered as to what ought to be done (*kiṃkartavyatāmūḍha*), characterized by joy, enthusiasm, wonder, and fear—one should go to whatever place [one intends]; there too, the perception is as previously taught. Thus it is taught.

Because, in states such as forgetfulness, one is characterized by a state of bewilderment regarding what ought to be done, which is indicative of the vast mass of delusion consisting of the failure to realize reality (tattva). (p. 73)

Having thus described the means for perceiving the Supreme Reality based on the waking state consisting of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [the author now addresses] that which is based on the waking state consisting of the activity of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*), since this will be discussed in the context of the passage: "For just as an object is seen indistinctly" (4.6ka). Now, therefore—
In order to demonstrate that state which is the locus of the waking condition, characterized by the activity of the organs of action, he says:
"or whatever place one may go while running, there [is the realization]. In that very place as well, there is the perception of vibration established in its own nature;
for there, because the distinctions between the functions of will, effort, cognition, and action are not perceived, there is the manifestation of the non-dual form of the Lord.

For instance, even while there exist specific functions such as the desire to lift the foot at every step, the exertion of effort, the determination of the location, and the act of placing the foot— all of which belong to one who is running—
consciousness remains established solely in its own undivided, supreme nature, because its internal distinctions are not being perceived, as if those functions were non-existent.
Then, being entirely under the control of another, the person enters the form of Īśvara.
This too should be understood as an indication of the activity of the organs of action, such as speech and so forth; thus, like one running— (p.
It is taught that even when the activity of speech is occupied with the utterance of exceedingly beautiful vowels and syllables,
or when the cluster of fingers is being most rapidly employed in the playing of the lute or flute,
one still perceives the vibration established therein— that is, within all the activities of the organs of action.

By the word "running," there is an indication [of other states as well]. For, in the verse beginning with "just as an object is seen indistinctly," he will demonstrate that this perception resides in the operation of the intellect and the sense organs. And although for every living being, in all states, the functions of all the senses do not occur without...
Although they are indeed capable of manifesting that state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) which throbs with the light of eternally arisen and established vibration (*spanda*), nevertheless,

for even the awakened one, that established vibration appears as if obscured by infinite particularities of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-viśeṣa*) arising in manifoldness through the power of the appearance of duality projected by the power of *māyā*.

Since it is impossible to indicate the state of being within the range of perception [of the Absolute], certain conditions such as extreme anger and so forth— which are suitable for its perception— are selected as means (*upāya*) and taught. And these, when reflected upon by one who is awakened, immediately serve as the means for attaining the perception of the established *spanda*.

They resort [to these states], but they are not experienced [as such], for that state consists precisely of suffering and the like. However, one who has emerged from it is awakened; by the power of instruction, he possesses a preeminent excellence of wisdom capable of discerning the true nature of the self as it truly is.
Through one-pointed cultivation of that very practice, he who has gradually ascended to the state of the perfectly awakened will experience the *spandatattva* (the principle of vibration);
he will experience it everywhere. This has been explained regarding that *spandatattva*.
Thus, in the commentary [on verse] 6.

Now, for the sake of perceiving the essential nature that has entered the fourth state (*turya-daśā*) which is dissolved within the waking function, he teaches three verses as an instruction on the means; therein, first, is a pair of verses:
"Whatever this [teacher] shall tell me, having taken hold of that state..."
Having formed the resolve, "I shall certainly do this," he remains.
Relying upon that [channel], both the moon and the sun set within the path of the *suṣumnā* by way of the upward path,
leaving behind the sphere of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Having resorted to— that is, having reached— that state indicated by the sentence characterized by the word "tām" (p.
76), both the moon and the sun— the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— of the person [merge] simultaneously.

They both set and dissolve. Having done what? By the very power of resorting to such a state, having abandoned the sphere of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—that is, having abandoned that body which is the cosmic egg, which is the sphere and the locus of its own expansion according to the principle "what is within is without"—and having transcended it due to the absence of any object of perception; by what path?
"Set" (*astamita*) means by way of the upward path (*ūrdhvamārga*), the entirely transcendent, supramundane way. And so it is said:

"In this twofold manner, having transcended its own object which is within the sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and having attained a state of neutrality (*madhyasthatā*) in that condition, it sets into its very cause. Likewise, that which is designated by the word "sun" (*sūrya*), consisting of the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The power of action (kriyā-śakti), having rendered void all the crooked movements characterized by the circulation through various channels (nāḍīs) and having attained the state of the universal vital breath (sāmānya-prāṇa), comes to rest in its own station via the path transcending the world. Therefore, he says that it has set upon the path of Suṣumṇā: "That channel named Suṣumṇā which occupies the center of the body..."

77) On that path—the flowing channel of the supreme power of the Lord—those two, becoming tranquil through the abandonment of the coloring of the object of knowledge and of activity, attain the state of being the supreme power itself; such is the meaning. Which [power] is that?

He says [this] with reference to the state (*daśā*): having resorted to, having fully taken hold of, and having firmly grasped that particular condition by means of which a person remains at some point in time, characterized by the complete cessation of all activity toward external objects and by the stabilization of all his powers. Having done what? "Having resorted to" (*samālambya*).
He states a sentence that culminates in another action preceded by the act of taking hold (*samālambana*):

"having thus resolved" (*iti saṃkalpya*), meaning having made such a resolution. How so? [It is] as follows: "Whatever this person tells me, I shall certainly do"; for by transgressing his command, there is immediately an undesirable consequence such as the loss of life.
The connection between the two verses is as follows: "This king or other person who falls upon me here is pointed out by the word 'this';

whatever matter he shall speak or say that it is my duty, I—having set aside all other tasks with my whole being—will certainly do it; I will accomplish it. This, however, is the intended meaning (*tātparya*): [The king or other person who falls upon me here is pointed out by the word 'this'. Whatever matter he shall speak or say that it is my duty, I—having set aside all other tasks with my whole being—will certainly do it; I will accomplish it. This is the connection between the two verses. But this is the intended meaning:

Because a person who has been prompted by someone of authority— due to some reason, by means of words that must necessarily be carried out, and with the intention of expressing a matter to be performed— is possessed of an intense concentration directed solely toward listening to those words.
When all mental fluctuations have subsided, consciousness necessarily enters the fourth state (*turyā*);

through the practice of reflecting upon that [state], the supreme reality is attained. In this context, the term "the sphere of the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍagocara*) denotes the space of the body, while the terms "moon" and "sun" denote the expansions of the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), respectively.

The purpose of this teaching is the attainment of rest in the supreme state— which transcends all external and internal paths— by the awakened one who has ascended to the pinnacle of the practice of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) upon the recognition of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*). This has been explained.
By [the author] Pṛthaktvavṛtti, [in the passage] beginning with "that state whose nature is vibration" (spandarūpām avasthām), etc.
And by the passage beginning with "his state" (tasya tāmavasthām) and so forth. || 8 ||
Now, one might object: "Since such a state arises somehow for everyone, what is the use of instruction? To this he says:
"Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved..."
Like one in the state of deep sleep, the deluded person becomes awakened and unobscured.

Then, at that time characterized by such a state, in the great void— the supreme space denoted by the term *sauṣumna-ādhvan*— because its essential nature is distinct from all objects of knowledge (*vedya*).

Furthermore, because it is distinct in nature from the elemental ether (*ākāśa*) whose quality is sound, what kind of own-being (*svasvabhāva*) is that which is indicated by the term "Great Ether" (*mahāvyoma*), wherein the moon and sun have dissolved and the entire expansion of the manifestation of knowledge and action has completely subsided? [It is] the state of the deluded one.

Due to the absence of the touch of the rays from the supreme power of the Supreme Lord, who is like the sun, there would be a collapse of the sleep of the cognition of bound souls (paśu) that does not awaken; it would be like the state of deep sleep (sauṣuptapada), as in the condition of deep sleep itself.
Just as the state of deep sleep, although its entire manifold of objects of knowledge has dissolved, remains for one who is unawakened at that time—

Due to the absence of the capacity for direct experience, this fourth state (*turya-daśā*) is likewise of the nature of delusion (*moha*). However, one who is awakened— awakened by the power of the descent of the Lord’s grace (*īśvara-śaktipāta*) to a preeminent degree that transcends the world, possessing the vision of correctly arisen right knowledge, and having experienced the fullness of the fourth state during the occasion of reflecting upon such a state— is truly enlightened.
"Unobstructed" means he would be free from, or attain freedom from, the obstruction consisting of the notion of "I" delimited by the body and so forth. This is what [the text] states.
This has been explained in the *Vṛtti* by the passage beginning with "In that great void" (*tasmin mahāvyomni*). (9)

Thus, it is precisely that power of Śaṅkara— the very Self— which has been established as having a single nature characterized solely by the perceiver persisting through all states, being distinct from the category of objects of knowledge such as the body, and for which the means of perception has been demonstrated.
Regarding the potency of mantras, which serve as the means for accomplishing the rites enjoined by the scriptures that must necessarily be performed—
the author states a pair of verses to instruct one who has already awakened and realized such a nature of the Self:
"Having seized that power, the mantras, possessing the power of the Omniscient One..."
They proceed toward their respective functions, like the sense organs of embodied beings.
Right there they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva. || 10 || 11 ||

For this reason—that is, by virtue of the explanation currently under discussion—these mantras, which consist of the arrangement of phonemes and so forth denoting the deity to be propitiated, possess the nature of Śiva;
that is, they share the unique qualities of the Supreme Lord Śiva, such as omniscience and the like.
The meaning is that those for whom that *dharma* exists are such that their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is non-different from Śiva. For what reason?

Having taken hold of power—that is, having accepted the capacity (*sāmarthya*) by means of the logical possibility of non-difference from Him during the state of the desire to utter [the mantra]—they are "praising" while possessing the strength of the Omniscient One, that is, by the power (*bala*) or capacity (*śakti*) of Śiva, who is endowed with the strength of omniscience.
They proceed toward their respective domains, extending themselves for the sake of sovereignty in accomplishing their own specific tasks.
For these [phonemes], as long as they have not attained the state of non-difference from the Supreme Lord, consist merely of letters subject to the properties of arising and perishing;
they are incapable of bending even a blade of grass. However, by ascending through the aforementioned power, they become assisted by fixed procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
They possess unimpeded power over the performance of their respective functions—both higher and lower—beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ending with the extraction of the poison of a scorpion.

If this is so, and since all mantras possess an equality of *vīrya* characterized by the aforementioned sequence of powers, then how can they have distinct spheres of authority? Why would they not all be authorized to accomplish every purpose?

In this regard, in order to establish that the very cause [of their operation] is being constrained by *niyati* (the principle of necessity) fashioned by the Supreme Lord, he provides an analogy: "How is it that these mantras proceed toward a restricted domain of authority? (p. 82).

For practitioners— just as for embodied beings who possess a body and so forth, whose sense of self-identity is fixed upon impermanent things such as the body alone, and who are all bearers of bodies— the instruments, namely the senses, [proceed] from the Supreme Lord alone, according to the reasoning established here in the passage beginning with "for this group of instruments."

Even though there is equality in their acquisition of activity, the cause for inducing consciousness, and so forth, the instruments—by the power of that imagined *niyati-śakti* (the power of necessity)—possess capacities that terminate solely in the illumination of their respective objects such as sound;
thus they proceed toward their own distinct functions, and not all [instruments] toward every [object]. It is exactly the same with these [individual souls].
Mantras function for practitioners who have realized the sense of "I" as having assumed the supreme nature, according to their specifically assigned authority;

therefore, like instruments, even though mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One, they have only fixed authorities. Consequently, mantras which possess the nature of Śiva, having been granted authority, are stainless (*nirañjana*).

They have emerged from the impurity (*mala*) consisting either of the coloring of the object of speech (*vācyoparāgarūpa*), which is like collyrium (*añjana*), or from that which consists of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of forms such as color; for this very reason, they are of a tranquil nature (*śāntarūpa*), for "tranquil" (*śānta*) means pure because nothing remains but pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*).

Those whose nature is the immutable form of the Self, being such, are completely dissolved right there in Śiva, the supreme cause, their own essential nature; they attain identity with Him. With what?
Together with the mind of the worshipper—that is, together with the mind of the practitioner—for in that [state]:

In the state [of realization], because it is free from the limiting conditions of intentional thought (*abhisandhi*), that mind of the practitioner remains as nothing but its own innate nature; with that [mind], what is established? This is what is established: the non-difference between the mantra and the consciousness during their states of arising and subsiding, due to their non-distinction from Śiva, the supreme cause.
Thus, as the very nature of mantra and as the nature of the practitioner's mind, Śiva-Śakti alone, having arisen assuming the forms of phonemes, volitions, and so forth,
now produces the delusion of duality for those practitioners who have not yet attained the realization of the touch of the power of their own true nature.

It culminates in the authority for accomplishing the definitive goal. However, for one who possesses a very firm self-realization within their own intrinsic nature exactly as it has been explained, and who knows the rising and setting [of all phenomena], all mantras [are effective] (p.
Mantras become capable of accomplishing all purposes without depending on specific procedures, auxiliary rites, or rules of application; for whatever word one utters with whatever intention,
that very word attains the state of an infallible mantra— thus, the mastery through the power of its own nature is established by itself.
The essential meaning is that the yogin must reflect upon the potency (*vīrya*) of mantras.

This should be understood as an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for by the reasoning already stated, it is not only mantras that possess the nature of Śiva, but rather there does not exist any action, knowledge, effect, or object of knowledge whatsoever that is not so.

Having attained its nature through the non-differentiation from the supreme reality, it does not become identical with Śiva—this he will state immediately thereafter. This has been explained in the *Vṛtti*:
"That power which is of the nature of unconditioned consciousness."
By such [passages] as this, || 11 ||
Thus ends the second flow, titled "The Perception of a Distinct Nature," in the Spandavivṛti composed by Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. || 2 ||
(p. 85) Now,
[the chapter] titled "The Establishment of the Power of the Universal Nature."
The third is the outflow.

Now, by way of presenting an alternative position, he speaks three verses to establish— through both reasoning and scriptural testimony— the point promised in the second half of the opening verse of this treatise: that Śiva, whose very nature is such, possesses the inherent character of manifesting the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) consisting of the manifestation of the universe.
Because the individual soul (jīva) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being; this is due to its realization of identity with them through the form of their cognition. || 1 ||
Therefore, among all reflections on the meaning of words, there is no state that is not Śiva;
the enjoyer alone is ever and everywhere established in the form of the object of enjoyment.
Or he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play—seeing thus and remaining constantly disciplined, he is undoubtedly liberated while living. || 3 ||

The connection is that he who possesses such consciousness is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). Thus, according to the manner just explained, that supreme practitioner who possesses *saṃvitti*— that is, perfect knowledge— is [liberated] constantly.

Uninterruptedly engaged in all states, composed, and with a one-pointed mind vigilant in the cultivation of the power of his own nature through the perspective of the teachings already stated and those yet to be told— he is liberated even while living, while still maintaining the vital breaths that have their locus in the fixed body.

Through the firm realization of the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) as one’s own essential nature—which is all-pervasive, the self of all, the Lord of all, and autonomous—one has emerged beyond birth and its opposites, becoming the Supreme Lord himself; regarding this matter, there is neither doubt nor delusion, because this reality is unshakable due to being personally experienced, logically established, and directly perceived. What does he do?

The one liberated while living perceives the entire, exhaustive, and infinite world—the universe variegated by the manifestation of endless entities—as mere play; he contemplates it as being nothing more than a sport fashioned from the toys of moving and unmoving beings created by himself.
For every person indeed...

One whose vision of stainless consciousness is capable of beholding the unmanifested nature of one's own self perceives this entire multitude of phenomena as distinct from oneself and from one another, and [sees] that they have arisen incessantly from some other cause.

Thinking thus, and experiencing the transformations of joy, sorrow, fear, and so forth born from that state of being, one repeatedly becomes a vessel for the bondage of birth and so on upon the path of worldly existence (*bhavādhvan*). But he who, according to the manner explained, has brought about the manifestation of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*), is like someone intent on play with things imagined by himself.

Just as one who plays with imitations of objects that serve as causes for fear, anger, and so forth does not undergo even the slightest turbidity of mental transformation such as fear because he knows their true nature (*yāthātmya*), in the same way,
knowing that things are merely the manifestation of the power of their own respective natures, the wise person does not undergo even the slightest transformation.

He attains [liberation]. Thus, seeing everything as nothing but play, he is liberated even while living. How is it that "he whose consciousness [is such]"? He explains this with the verse beginning with "by that," etc.: by that reason which is about to be stated, there is no state whatsoever among the contemplations of word and meaning that is not Śiva—he who possesses such consciousness is liberated while living.

Thus: "Word" (*śabda*) is a collection of words that conveys meaning; "meaning" (*artha*) is the multitude of entities to be expressed, which is manifold due to distinctions such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth; "reflection upon these two" (*tayoḥ cintā*) refers to conceptualizations (*vikalpanā*) in their various forms, arising from the coloring [of the mind] by the infinite objects of reflection.

The various cognitions that constitute worldly transaction— within these reflections on words and meanings— there is no such state or condition whatsoever, whether in the form of reflection on words or reflection on meanings, that does not directly become Śiva Himself. Since this is so, the enjoyer, the very experiencer, is the Lord (Īśvara) always, eternally, everywhere, and in all states.

Existing as the nature of the object of enjoyment—that is, as the very essence of the thing to be experienced—there is no separate entity called "the enjoyed" whatsoever; this form consisting of the division between enjoyer and enjoyed is merely a manifestation of the failure to reflect upon reality. For what reason? [He asks: "Is there any state that is not Śiva? He says: because the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the Self, consists of all things.

The meaning is that even the worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the cognition of mutually distinct objects, is established only on the basis of the non-difference between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*). Why is this so?
Because all things arise from the realization of identity (*tādātmya*) through the nature of their cognition (*saṃvedana*).

The individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything; by reason of its nature—which is the cognition or knowledge of any object of consciousness such as a jar or pleasure—the realization of identity arises from that cause, namely, the consciousness of non-difference. From that [realization], it proceeds...

That which is the source of all things—the arising of all entities—is therefore the soul (*jīva*) consisting of everything. What is meant by this? When the empirical functioning of the soul itself is investigated, it establishes the true nature of reality. For instance, this [soul], while indeed cognizing its own object...

It brings forth and creates; for an object attains its own nature only while being perceived, and not while unperceived. And this state of being perceived is the state of shining forth in this or that form.
Furthermore, this state of shining forth is not distinct from the Light (prakāśa); it is nothing other than that. As the proponent of Nyāya has said:
"Because it is felt through volition, and because that which is not of its nature is not felt.
And thus, whatever this living being perceives, each of those becomes his very body; it is not, however, restricted to a specific configuration of parts such as a head and hands.
p.

90) For even that [body] becomes his body only during the state of being perceived; at other times, however, it is merely an external object. And thus, because of the commonality of being perceived, two kinds of bodies are traditionally taught for him.
According to those who know reality, that which consists of the elements and that which consists of the mental states—

due to the power of the majesty of *māyā* having caused the true nature (*tāttvika-svabhāva*) to be forgotten— at the moment of perceiving an object, this individual soul (*jīva*), its capacity being closed up due to a lack of self-reflection, exists as the locus of a limited egoity (*avacchinna-ahaṃkāra*).

That which he perceives as a body possessing a head, hands, and so forth, is said to consist of the elements (*bhūta-ātmaka*), because it is composed of the [five] emanations (*sṛṣṭi*) and so on. However, that which he perceives as distinct through the objects of sound and so forth is of the nature of existence (*bhāva-ātmaka*). But when both are investigated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), both are his body.

Because there is no difference in the fact that they are being experienced. Thus, in the state of union with existence characterized by being experienced, the individual soul (jīva), although existing as consisting of all things and possessing the universal form due to its non-difference from the object of experience, [remains as such] because of the non-emergence of the reflective awareness of the reality of experiencing those objects; therefore, all this...
By distinguishing [the self] through its distinctness from other things— both from other causes that have acquired their own nature apart from the self, and from [other selves] mutually—

And the transmigrating soul (*jīva*), identifying itself through the ego-sense with impermanent states such as the body and so forth, and thus subject to the bondage of birth and other conditions, is designated as such. But when,
through the falling of the rays of the power of the sun that is Śiva, the clear vision awakened by that awakening becomes manifest, [the soul is liberated].

When [the Self] becomes manifest through the powers of perceiving and reflecting upon objects as they truly exist, then that very [Self] becomes Śiva, who consists of a wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) manifesting the manifold universe merely through volition (*saṃkalpa*). Therefore it has been said:
"The realization of identity [with the object] occurs by the power of the nature of perceiving each respective object."

Because there is a consciousness of the non-difference of the object being experienced [from the subject], all things arise; therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything. By that reason—namely, the realization of its own nature as consisting of everything—there is no state whatsoever that does not consist of Śiva. Consequently, the enjoyer himself is eternally the Lord, in the form of the objects of enjoyment and as the nature of the entities to be governed.
He is established everywhere; thus, for one who possesses such consciousness, he is "liberated while living"—this is for the purpose of synthesizing the meaning of the sequence of statements. (p.

This has been restated: by these three verses, the existence of the Self alone as the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) is established, since no other cause for the manifold universe (*viśvaprapañca*) is logically possible. As it has been said by the knower of Brahman:
"The divine Self, by its own power of illusion (*māyā*), fashions itself from itself through itself."
"That very [Self] perceives through differentiation"—this is the settled conclusion of the Vedānta.
Thus it has been said by another as well, by way of praise:
"Though You remain external through various limiting conditions (*upādhi*), Your manifold variety is spoken of like that of crystal and the like;
for if they were ever, in any way, or anywhere capable of existing apart from Your manifestation, [they would not appear so]."

Or let the universe be held by the best of the wise to be either an illusory transformation (*vibhrama*) resulting from the maturation of atoms, or a manifestation (*vivarta*); for if such conceptual constructions were yours, your own power would not be able to establish them in that way.

Thus, here too, O Śiva, you alone shine as the jewel consisting of pure consciousness; though you possess a manifold orb of rays in the form of the conceptualizations of opening and closing that flash at every moment, you nevertheless manifest with a most pure body as the wondrous sole ground of all.
93) This has been explained in the Vṛtti: this very Self is indeed of the nature of all things, each individually.
By such [words] as "by him" and "of such a kind," and so forth.
And by the passage beginning with "evam svabhāve yasya" (in this way, for one whose intrinsic nature... and so forth. || 1 || 2 || 3 ||

Thus ends the third outflow (*niṣyanda*), titled "The Proof that the Universe is Nothing but the Power of One's Own Essential Nature," in the *Spandavivṛti* composed by the venerable Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. || 3 ||
(p. 94) Now, [the section] called "The Perception of Non-Difference."
The fourth is the outflow.
Now, in order to demonstrate that this very realization, when properly grasped, is the means for perceiving non-duality—
and to establish that it effects all ritual purifications such as the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and so forth— it is said:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator."
It is the attainment of identity with that [deity] for the practitioner who so desires. (1)

The arising (*udaya*) of that certain object of meditation— a specific deity to be remembered in various forms and expressed by mantras— is its manifestation in those various forms of worship, which possess unfailing power capable of accomplishing their respective purposeful actions; in what locus?— in the mind of the meditator, that is, in the mind belonging to the one who meditates and remembers.

In this regard, what is this "arising" (*udaya*) in the context of conceptualization? It is that which is established through the power of the object for a practitioner who is intent, desiring to utter a mantra while remaining in the state of desire (*icchāvasthā*). (p. 95)

"Attainment of identity with that" (*tadātmatā-samāpatti*) means: the essence (*ātman*) of that object of meditation is its own nature (*svarūpa*); the state of being that is "identity with that" (*tadātmatā*); and "attainment" (*samāpatti*) is becoming one with it. The intended meaning here is as follows: at the stage when there is a desire to utter a mantra for the purpose of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, [the practitioner's mind] has the form of another deity obstructed by the mantra.

That state of non-differentiation which is spontaneously accomplished by the mind of the practitioner without effort is itself the primary arising of the deity to be worshipped, in the form of direct perception for the meditator whose consciousness is capable of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); it is not, however, a state where the form is perceived as something separate— since through this very consciousness, one attains the nature of Śiva.
"Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva"—
this injunction finds its fulfillment through this very [means] by way of that realization.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of these and other [passages]. || 1 ||
He states that this very consciousness is what purifies through other ritual injunctions:
"This alone is the attainment of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva. (2)

96) This very [knowledge], as previously explained, arises from the eradication of false cognition— which consists in the perception of objects to be known as distinct from self-luminous consciousness, and which takes the form of the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) directed toward perishable things such as the body.

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), which consists in the realization of the single reality that is the unconditioned, pure, and spontaneous nature itself, is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and the attainment of the immortal (*amṛta-prāpti*). Indeed, the "attainment of the immortal" is the realization of the Self (*ātman*) who is Śiva—imperishable and immortal; it is not the attainment of some specific material substance that is insentient and transient.

The attainment of some entity is the "attainment of immortality" (*amṛtaprāpti*), for that is the cause of the soul’s possessing a body that persists over time; it is spoken of thus by way of metaphor. Likewise, this very [state] is the "seizing of the self," which is the consciousness (*saṃvit*) occurring in the moment of the desire to utter the mantra in such a manner; this is the seizing of the self, that is, of the living soul (*jīva*).

"Seizing" (*graha*) means grasping; for in various specific ritual procedures such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, the seizing of either the self or the disciple is taught in the scriptures. As it is cited in the *Vṛtti*:
"At the time of initiation, the Guru should perform the seizing of the self through his intellect."

Thus, the attainment of non-difference with one's own nature, which is the supreme cause, that arises for the Self when it assumes a specific form imagined for the sake of accomplishing such an injunction— when that [attainment] is being reflected upon...

It brings about the perfection of the rite consisting of the grasping of the Self, and not otherwise; for the grasping of that formless [Self] is impossible, because it is non-different from the grasper, the Supreme Self, whose nature is all-pervasive consciousness. Likewise, this alone is the initiation of Nirvāṇa; Nirvāṇa is cessation, resulting from the complete exhaustion of the agitation characterized by dualistic cognition.

Ultimate peace is the consciousness’s abiding in its own essential nature. For that purpose, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the bestowal of awakening to one's true nature and characterized by the destruction of the bondage of duality.
And this very initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) is what has been explained here as consciousness itself, because it is the cause of that [peace]. For this [consciousness]...

Consciousness (saṃvit) bestows the true being of Śiva; that which is the true being—the existence—of Śiva, who is the Supreme Lord, his very own essential nature, in the form of which [he says], "I alone am" (p.

Thus, this uncontradicted practice is established as being valid in the state of attainment; it is the bestower and the means of realization, for it is that unsurpassed *saṃskāra* which is the domain of the perfectly awakened Guru. It consists solely in the attainment of one's own nature, which is identical with Paramaśiva, and does not consist of specific ritual procedures to be accomplished through external means. This has been explained.
"This very [is it] for one who is devoid of false knowledge," and so forth, in the commentary (vṛtti). || 2 ||

Having thus established that this consciousness is the cause of the performance of the supreme ritual procedure, he now speaks two verses to demonstrate its status as the cause of other supernatural accomplishments (*siddhi*) by means of an illustration from the worldly transactions of transmigrating beings: "Just as the Creator, when entreated by desire, [manifests] objects situated in the heart of the waking person..."
Having brought about the rising of the moon and the sun, he brings [liberation] to embodied beings.
Likewise, because it never oversteps the bounds of affection, it will surely manifest the desired objects even in dreams,
appearing clearly and constantly in the interim.
p.
99) Just as for every transmigrating being who perceives the mere body of the embodied one as the self, there exists in the heart the waking state—
characterized by the activity of the sense-faculties busily engaged in grasping their respective objects— as he experiences that state while awake.

When requested by his own will— that is, impelled by the desire to see those desired objects existing and established within his own intention— the Supreme Lord, the Creator and Maker of all, the Paramātman, brings them into being as if entreated; for through the power of the nature of those states, he accomplishes that object by means of attaining identity with it.

"Having brought about the arising of the eyes according to one's intention—the manifestation of the essential nature consisting solely in the ascertainment of the intended object"—this is the sentence of comparison (*upamāna*). The intended meaning here is this: whichever transmigrating being [perceives] whatever object...

When the desire to see arises, in that state of longing to behold Him, he suddenly and involuntarily enters into the Supreme Self, the Creator, non-differently; that state is metaphorically designated as his "prayer," because the attainment of the desired object is preceded by it.

Requested by her, the Creator (dhātṛ), for the purpose of manifesting that specific object alone, brought about through the medium of his attentive nature the arising of the eyes characterized by the manifestation of their own form, even though many other visible objects were present.

He demonstrates that very object which was requested solely out of a desire to see it, and nothing else. The phrase "having brought about the arising of the eyes" is to be understood as a mere illustration; by this, one who is requested to listen brings about the arising of the ears and causes [the teacher] to hear only that which was desired to be heard, even when other things worthy of hearing are present.

The phrase "the Ordainer of embodied beings" is to be applied to all the sense organs as well. Furthermore, by representing the two eyes through the terms "Soma" and "Sūrya," the purpose is to demonstrate the actual non-difference of the individual soul from the Ordainer (Dhātṛ), who is the universal form.
And this has been explained by the author of the commentary itself for the sake of illustration.

Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by means of attention toward the eyes and so forth," the manifestation of all objects for all living beings occurs preceded by will;
and that state of will in the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), being non-different in form from the Supreme Cause, is thus the Supreme Lord himself, who is autonomous.
"This entire [reality] manifests according to its will" (p.
thus, those transmigrating beings who are delimited by bodies and so forth produced by His power of *māyā* do not realize that ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
But as for the awakened one,
whose sword of wisdom has been sharpened on the whetstone of the excellence of practicing the aforementioned instructions and who has severed the bonds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—
he is capable of recognizing that [Self] even when it is being recalled; thus, the yogi of non-differentiated samādhi is established.

This is taught by means of the sentence containing the object of comparison: just as, when entreated by their desire according to the reasoning established by them [the Naiyāyikas], He expands all objects, in that very same manner, eternally and at all times— in every state involving the relationship between the knower and the known— He manifests Himself during the state of *praṇaya*, which is the state of desire.
Because he does not transgress— that is, does not violate— the aspiration consisting of the realization of identity with Him,

and because he does not neglect it due to his constant attentiveness toward that reflective awareness, [the Lord bestows all things] even during sleep; for even when the eyes and other senses have ceased their activity,
in the state of deep sleep where the objects are His own creations perceivable by the mind alone, He grants everything desired as long as it is sought.

Having made manifest even those very objects desired by the practitioner most clearly and most openly, this Creator, situated in the center and always seated within the heart, [bestows them] necessarily and with certainty.

"One should reveal" means "one should propagate"—this is the meaning of the illustrative sentence beginning with "tathā" (thus). Furthermore, the intended sense (*tātparya*) is as follows: because he is ever-attentive through moment-to-moment reflective awareness, [the yogi] maintains that intimacy (*praṇaya*) characterized by absorption into his own nature—the very essence of the Creator, the Lord of All—which is established by his own power within all experiences at all times.

The Creator does not overstep him; even in dreams, He reveals only those objects that are agreeable to him, as if he were awake. For him, the objects of the dream do not manifest by their own independence as an obstruction to His own power characterized by universal agency—since He is beyond saṃsāra—but rather, He remains independent.
By its own power, it creates those [objects] as it desires. As Bhartṛhari has said:
"Having divided itself by itself and created various kinds of entities, the Lord of All, possessing all powers, becomes the enjoyer within a dream."

Thus, for this very reason, it has been said that this is the sovereignty of dream; there is no distinction between that [dream] and waking—this is what was meant by the breaking through the veil of darkness. It is the obstruction of one's own unconditioned majesty produced by the egoity of the body and so forth.
*Tamas* is that which veils, covers, and conceals one's own nature; its *nirbheda*— meaning its destruction through the manifestation of one's own infinite majesty— is what emerges in that state.
This has been explained individually in the *Vṛtti* by the passage beginning with "of this [consciousness],
whose own nature is unmanifest," and so forth; likewise:
By the passage beginning with "Even in a dream, he sees only desired objects," and so forth. || 3 || 4 ||
Now, demonstrating that the yogin is equal to those in saṃsāra merely by emerging from such a samādhi, [the author] speaks in order to strengthen the firmness of his constant union:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent, because it would possess that nature."
It is constant, just like that of a worldly person in the two states of waking and dreaming.
Otherwise, however, in a manner different from the one described above, this [universe] belongs to me alone—the one Supreme Lord, the independent creator of all.

For the yogin who exists in the form of the absence of the perception that "this is the work of the world," during both the states of waking and dreaming— the two stages of wakefulness and sleep— creation, which is the construction of various mental objects, would be eternally independent in its true nature because it consists of the qualities of emanation (*sarga*) due to the arising of the consciousness of the reality of the Self.

If it were not perceived as having the agency of its own independent self alone, it would become a source of manifold delusions, acting according to its own will, with an unstoppable expansion of such power. Of whom?
Just like that of the worldly person, the transmigrating world—as is the case there. This is the intended meaning here:

The two stages characterized by waking and sleeping constitute the nature of emanation (*sarga*); for it is therein that the abiding of the Supreme Lord’s power is established through the relationship of knowledge and the object of knowledge. In such a dual stage, whatever yogi may arise—even while not abandoning the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the aforementioned consciousness—he remains entirely independent.
For one who is well-established in his own self as the agent of all,
those two states whose nature is emission (sṛṣṭi) are not capable of obstructing his power; however, he who is otherwise than this [is subject to them].

The meaning is that one must remain constantly disciplined as a yogi, thinking: "I am being rendered subject to another by this very creation of phenomenal existence (*bhāvasṛṣṭi*), which is merely a worldly appearance. This [occurs] otherwise, in the absence of abiding in one's true nature (*svarūpa*).
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by such passages as "ityādi" and so forth. || 5 ||
Now, through this very consciousness, the knowledge of objects that are past, future, concealed, or remote becomes easily attainable—
just as an object seen indistinctly, even when the mind is attentive,
shines forth with even greater clarity when cultivated by the exertion of its own power. (6)
Thus, having mastered that which exists in its ultimate sense, in whatever place, by whatever means, and in whatever manner,
it proceeds forth before long.

For just as when someone’s mind is attentive and possesses an intense effort born of the desire to see that object, even though the object has been seen instantaneously, it appears and manifests indistinctly and unmanifestly; and immediately thereafter, [it becomes clear].

Cultivated through the exertion of one's own power— that is, the strength and capacity of one's own self, characterized by omniscience and other such qualities— the effort (*udyoga*) being the enthusiasm for vision through most intense concentration— one who is thus cultivated and characterized shines forth more clearly; having all particularities recognized without exception, he manifests as "this is that very one."

—This is the sentence of comparison. Its purport is as follows: when any desired object is not clearly perceived by one whose eyes have merely been opened for an instant, yet later, at another moment, it appears much more clearly to that very same person while remaining in that same place with their eyes fixed intently upon it—what is the cause of this?
For he does not bring forward any means for perceiving particulars that is distinct from the act of seeing; therefore, there is no penetration into the ultimate nature [of things].

In this very way, it arises for him that through the touch of his own power, that object manifests in its true nature; therefore, for all embodied beings, the sole means for the manifestation of all objects is the exertion of one's own power alone, and nothing else.
Although such a manifestation of objects is common to all living beings, it belongs only to the awakened yogin.

When reflected upon, that reality shines forth in such a way for [the yogi], but not for another whose right vision is obscured by the darkness of *māyā*; thus, by this instruction expressed in the illustrative sentence beginning with "in this manner," the yogi alone is reminded of the truth. For just as an object seen indistinctly, having overcome its own [latent] power...

It manifests even more clearly: in this very manner described by the sentence of the analogy, for the yogin who, having overcome his own power (*bala*)— that is, the capacity of his own nature— at the moment of the desire to see, abides by presiding over it non-differently, [the object appears] in that same way,
through that very mode which is not inconsistent with its respective state, form, place, time, and so forth.
It proceeds, it attains perfect manifestation, and it becomes fully present as an object of knowledge. What is that thing? That which, in the ultimate sense, exists in reality.

An entity, such as a cow or the like, exists in whatever state, by whatever mode, with whatever specific form—such as possessing a dewlap and other characteristics—and in whatever place, whether distant or remote, or at whatever time, such as the past; it proceeds exactly in that manner. This is the underlying meaning here: when an object is perceived in an indistinct manner, its...

When the reasoning that remains uncontradicted is established— that for anyone who has awakened through the practice of reflecting upon that [reality], the non-difference from the very nature of omniscience arises effortlessly so as to produce a most vivid manifestation, and he knows objects as they are intended, even those separated by space, time, and so forth, according to their true essence— then [the conclusion follows].
This alone is the cause for the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience. Therefore it has been said:
"Knowledge of limited objects regarding the past and future is not at all wonderful, because its own nature is unobscured."
Thus [it is said]. For in that state, the power of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), unimpeded by space, time, and so forth, becomes manifest.
This should be understood as an elliptical expression for the statement "an object is seen indistinctly"; therefore, the same principle should be applied to hearing and the other [senses] as well.

And by this— namely, through the entry into the established vibration (*pratiṣṭhitaspanda*) which is accomplished during a particular state of effort for the sake of the clearer perception of objects such as the visible—
the means for attaining the supreme reality (*paratattva*) is provided, which is based upon the waking state consisting of the operations of all the faculties of cognition and action.
It should be understood as having been established incidentally; for the author of the commentary has explained these two verses individually,
beginning with the words "Just as one standing at a distance," and so forth.
Likewise, by that very same specific effort, and so forth, according to the passage beginning with [the word] "ityādinā" (and so on). || 6 || 7 ||
Now, by this very same reasoning, in order to demonstrate the conquest of hunger, thirst, and so forth, he says: "Since even one who is weak, having mastered that [hunger], proceeds to his task;
likewise, one who is excessively hungry should suppress his hunger. (8)

Because, for this reason, having seized his own power— the capacity characterized by universal agency and sovereignty— and remaining inseparable from it through the previously stated reasoning, even one who is weak [becomes powerful].

"Because his bodily constituents have been diminished, even though he is incapable, someone engages in an activity such as the labor of carrying a burden and becomes intent upon action"—this is the illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavākya*). Its intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as follows:
one who, due to having an emaciated body, is indeed powerless, yet begins an activity such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) through the power of practice...
Even when confronted by a much stronger external object, one is able to perform actions such as physical exertion;

in the arising of such capacity, there is no cause whatsoever other than the overcoming of the power of one's own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), according to the reasoning previously explained. That [power], moreover, is the strength characterized by the ability to act as the agent of all things according to one’s will, which belongs to the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).

The illusory agent, because his power is bound by *māyā*, considers his capacity to accomplish a specific effect to depend upon other specific causes; yet even he, in a state of unimpeded enthusiasm, thinking "I am able to do this," relies upon that very power.
"He becomes capable of accomplishing that task"—this reasoning is within the scope of the yogin's own realization;
taking this as an illustration (p.

This very point is taught with reference to him by means of the following illustrative statement: just as even one who is weak becomes capable of accomplishing a task that requires strength solely by resorting to the power of his own nature,
so too, in that same manner, by resorting to his own power— which is independent in accomplishing all tasks— he [acts] through his own inherent capacity.

He who, having taken hold [of this power], is exceedingly hungry—overwhelmed by an intense desire for food—should cover, conceal, or subdue that hunger; for, by manifesting the capacity of his own innate nature which is eternally satisfied and uncreated, the very act of consuming food and drink becomes the cause for the cessation of hunger and other such effects. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that when the obstruction caused by the power of *niyati* (destiny) has been shattered, one should completely cause that [power] to disappear, so that one becomes eternally satisfied—
even if one is weak and one's vital constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth). || 8 ||

Having thus established the various logical proofs for the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience and omnipotence individually, [the author] once again demonstrates them by means of a single illustrative proof.
To explain these [powers], he says:
"Just as omniscience and the rest [arise] when the body is presided over by this [power], so too will it be everywhere through the presiding over one's own self. (9)

When this self, as the thinker, presides over and inhabits the body through the realization of "I," then omniscience and all other qualities— namely, those attributes such as agency and the rest, of which knowledge (the state of being a knower) is the first— which have the body as their locus, and all objects of knowledge and effects, abide in that [self] as they do in everyone else.

This is the illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavākya*). Its purport is as follows: whatever this Self presides over through the cognition "I am," that becomes its body; and all that—whether gross or subtle, whether the object of knowledge or the object of action—it knows and performs. By means of this illustration, it is shown that it is exactly in that same manner.

By means of the "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*)— through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as the locus of the body— upon one's own self, which is one's own true nature (*svasvabhāva*), characterized as being free from pain and pleasure and so forth, and whose essence is pure, non-dual consciousness distinct from the body and other such things;
thus [is established] the entire range of knowable objects and effects that have the body as their substratum.
p.

113) Just as [the state of] being a knower and so forth [is universal], so too will omniscience and other qualities necessarily manifest for the yogin throughout all worlds, even within all [limited] bodies, because [his nature] is characterized by the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) which is distinct from the mere body and its mutual differences.
The meaning is that omniscience and the other qualities are indeed manifested everywhere.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the passage beginning with "by this nature of the self" (*ātmasvabhāvena*). || 9 ||
Thus, he states the logical argument for the eradication of disease, wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth:
"Illness is a ravager of the body, and its course is within ignorance;
if it is destroyed by the unfolding of that [knowledge], how could it exist without a cause? (10)
Glanis is the loss of joy produced by lethargy and the like; it is a ravager within the body,

forcibly seizing the constituents (dhātus), strength, complexion, luster, vitality, and so forth, and it arises from ignorance due to the absence of understanding the reality as it has been explained.

(114) *Sṛtiḥ* means wandering or active manifestation; that [state] is ignorance (*ajñāna*). If it is "destroyed by the unfolding" (*unmeṣaviluptam*)—that is, if it is destroyed, severed, and reduced to rootlessness by the "unfolding," which is the expansion of the light of one's own nature (*svabhāvāloka*) to be described hereafter—then that [state] is lassitude (*glāni*).
