How could that which is causeless and devoid of a reason come into being? It would certainly not exist, because there is no arising of that which is without a sign (*nirnimitta*). That which is called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is the conceit of a self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth, which are the substrata for transformations such as birth, transformation, growth, decay, and death; and when this [conceit] exists, a person remains unawakened.

Superimposing its transformations—birth and so forth—upon the Self, one is dragged down by exhaustion; but for one in whom the realization of the true Self has arisen through the cultivation of the "unfolding" (unmeṣa) to be described hereafter, whence can there be exhaustion?
Thus, the primary fruit [of this practice] consists in the cessation of the loss of innate bliss (sahajānanda).

(115) Having explained that the absence of weariness (*glāni*) is primary, whereas the absence of wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth is secondary— since, at that time, from what cause could such weariness arise, being devoid of its cause— the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) has further explained it as follows.
For this very reason, yogis are free from wrinkles and grey hair, and possess firmness of body. || 10 ||
Now, in order to explain the true nature of *unmeṣa*, which is the cause for the destruction of ignorance—the very cause of exhaustion—he says:
"That from which, for one intent upon a single thought, there arises the emergence of another, should be known as *unmeṣa*; one should perceive it by oneself. (11)
That "re-emergence," moreover, is to be known, understood, and characterized as the expansion of the manifestation of one's own essential nature. What is it?

It is [the state] of one who is intent upon a single thought—that is, while a single thought is being perceived—arising from the illumination of one's own essential nature, which serves as the cause, consisting of a consciousness that is not colored by the manifestation of the object of thought.

There would arise— that is, there would be the production— of another cognition, namely a subsequent thought that takes [that first cognition] as its apprehended object; and the yogi would perceive that [subsequent cognition] by himself, through his own self, as the Supreme Lord in the ultimate sense, entirely distinct from everything else.

One should realize: "I am this Supreme Cause, the Supreme Self. For its essential nature cannot be characterized as "this" (idantayā), like sound and other objects, because its very being is known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Even though it is eternally manifest, it is revealed at that very moment to the one for whom it is being taught.

The designation "unmeṣa" (opening) has been employed. However, one might think as follows: "When a certain thought exists, the arising of another thought occurs; that very thought is the cause of the subsequent thought, and there is no other intervening entity to be perceived—distinct from the nature of the two thoughts—that could serve as the cause of the second thought."

This connection between the two thoughts—consisting of the state of being an antecedent cause and the state of being an effect, which are conceived as occurring in a temporal sequence—is not established without a third party who synthesizes them; for [otherwise] the prior would merely be a cause.

Furthermore, there is another reflection consisting of an effect: he who synthesizes [the two], and that synthesizer who is undeniable, is the very Self—the cause of all—whose nature is pure consciousness alone, pervading the duality of the reflection to be synthesized; thus He is called *unmeṣa* (the unfolding). For this very reason, it has been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti*:
"Experienced as pervasive at the conclusion of the two types of thought," and so forth. || 11 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate the power of the practice of *unmeṣa*, he says that for yogins who are generally intent upon specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), those very *siddhis* which are desired as the fruits to be attained are, for one practicing this [practice], merely a succession of obstacles.
From this [state] the drop (bindu), from this the sound (nāda), from this form (rūpa), and from this the flavor (rasa) proceed very quickly toward the embodied soul as agents of agitation. 12.
Therefore, from this aforementioned unfolding (*unmeṣa*),
by means of an uninterrupted attentiveness during the states of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth occurring in conditions such as waking,
[one perceives] that which is momentary, perishable, diverse, dependent, and trivial in nature.

By meditating upon the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the object to be known— which serves as the cause of all— these signs of accomplishment will, in a short time, that is, after a brief period, arise as disturbances; they function as provocations of the mind by means of satisfaction, pride, arrogance, and so forth.
For the embodied yogi whose sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth has not been completely uprooted, these things proceed—that is, they manifest. What are they?

They are: *bindu*—that particular radiance which arises from the practice of meditation on the region between the eyebrows and other such places, increasing further and further through the excellence of meditative practice, and which results from the practice of piercing the *bindu*.

It is manifested for those who meditate upon the *dhara-tattva*. Thus: the *nāda*, beginning with a sound as thick as the roar of a rushing river or a thundercloud, gradually becomes subtle and manifests as an imitation of the humming of bees intoxicated by honey, once it has been uttered by itself.

This particular sound which those practicing the principle of space (vyomatattva) hear; likewise, that perception of the forms of various visible objects even when there is an obstruction such as dense darkness,
by those whose minds are fixed on the principle of fire (tejastattva)— [meaning, by another eye, that is, in its entirety].
p.

119) They behold it. Likewise—the taste of nectar (*amṛta*) [is experienced] even in the absence of a flavorful object by those intent on the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) such as *lolāgra* (the tip of the tongue) and *lambikā* (the uvula), which are held at the mouth. [Note: *lolāgra* refers to the root of the tongue; *lambikā* refers to the cavity of the palate.]

It should be understood here that even that specific quality of touch which is perceived by those meditating on the principle of air (*pavanatattva*), and which is manifested for those meditating on the principle of air, proceeds from this [source]. This is the intended meaning here:

for the yogi who practices the expansion (*unmeṣa*), these [powers], though difficult to attain through long-term practice of various concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) and the like, are attained without delay.
One should not remain fixed upon these perceptions, for they constitute obstacles to ascending to the state beyond all expression (*niruttara-pada*).

Although these [perceptions] occur sequentially for other yogins, for those practicing the yoga of *unmeṣa* (the upward opening), they proceed even non-sequentially due to the absence of such intentional focus; thus they have been described accordingly. This has already been explained.
Therefore, [the author] says "from this unfolding," and so forth, in the commentary. || 12 ||
p.

120) Having thus, by means of the instruction on *unmeṣa*, concisely established that the nature of the Self is distinct from the body and other objects of cognition— a point already demonstrated through many previous methods— he now [establishes] that very same [nature] as proven by the self-evident experience of all people.

Having made conventional usage the means of demonstration and briefly establishing the state of universal form (viśvarūpatā), he states the essential purport of the entire treatise: "When [the Self], as if desiring to see all objects, remains pervading them..."
Then, what is the use of much speaking? One will understand it for oneself.

When, at that time, the practitioner— out of a desire to see, as it were, having pervaded all objects, that is, all entities that have entered the sphere of cognition, by the light of his own self-awareness and having made them dissolve within it,
remains established in a single reality through the cessation of the delusion of perceiving multiplicity— at that time, in that state...
Regarding the fruit that is experienced during a *daśā*, what is the use of such extensive and abundant verbal descriptions of those fruits?
121) Even if thousands of books were composed with the desire to explain them, they would be useless for that purpose.

Because it transcends the range of verbal expression, he says: "He himself will realize that. That such a fruit will be attained by oneself, by one's own self, independent of any external means; for it is to be personally experienced (*svasaṃvedya*) by the practitioner.
The intended meaning here is this: by a yogi who desires to know that all phenomena are non-different from their own intrinsic nature.

The state of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), which has been personally experienced, must be illustrated as follows: at that time, the objects desired to be seen abide without distinction from their own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), because there is no emergence of the cognition of "this-ness" (*idantā-pratyaya*), which is the cause for the differentiation of objects.
Thus, in the state of the desire to see, there is non-difference between the objects sought to be seen and the essential nature of the knower (*kṣetrajña*).

Likewise, there is indeed non-difference between the nature of the Supreme Self and all the entities of the world— this [truth] is addressed specifically to the yogi whose eye of discernment has been opened by the practice of reflecting upon the realization of the nature of the Self as distinct from what was previously taught, and who is thus capable of perceiving the moment of the desire to see [the truth].

This is the instruction: for one whose vision of right knowledge is obscured by the cataract of conceptual construction produced by the power of *māyā*, the reality of the Self—which is in truth a single, undivided essence of pure consciousness—is [concealed].

Perceiving things as having manifold forms through the distinction of subjects and the distinction of objects, they construct a conceptual division of states such as "desire to see," "being seen," and "having been seen"; yet,
they are unable to grasp that even for those things they desire to see, there is an ontological non-difference from the nature of the living being (*jīva*).

How could they realize the non-difference of the phenomena of the world from the nature of the Supreme Self? Only by means of the yogi— who, through the method of reflecting upon the moment of his own desire to see [the truth], contemplates the non-difference of his own nature with the manifestations of all worldly phenomena.
One must become like a sun that shatters the darkness of duality.

This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the passage beginning with "the desire to see" (*didṛkṣā*), meaning the wish to see, as if one were situated in that very state [of seeing]. || 13 ||
In order to strengthen this very instruction, he says (p.
"The awakened one should always remain, having examined the field of experience through knowledge."
One should concentrate everything in one place; then one will not be oppressed by anything else.

At all times and in all states of experience, one should remain awakened; because of being intent on the practice of the taught instructions, with the vision of right knowledge unblinking, one should abide as if waking. How so?—having observed, discerned, and ascertained the object of perception through knowledge—that is, through conscious awareness—as being of such-and-such a nature, [one should rest] in the single Knower.
The meaning is that one should superimpose— that is, offer— all objects of cognition within one's own self, realizing them as non-different from it.
Consequently, through this act of superimposition— which consists in the realization of the non-difference of all entities from the nature of the single cognizer—
one [is freed] from the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that appear as distinct, such as the multitude of entities consisting of *kalā* and so forth, which will be described later.
One is not afflicted—that is, one is not bound and tormented within the wheel of saṃsāra by the noose consisting of the realization of a perishable self-identity and so forth.
This is the intended meaning here.

Whatever object, such as form and so forth, the cognizer perceives and determines through visual and other cognitions, that very object becomes non-different from the nature of the cognizer at the stage of determination. For what is called "determination" is simply the state of the thing being manifest; and since it is manifest, it is non-different [from the light], for it cannot be otherwise.

For if it were of a nature distinct from light, its manifestation would be impossible. Thus, in the state of certainty, the non-difference of all entities from the subject, whose essential nature is pure light, is established by their very being; therefore, although this relationship between the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping exists, when it is not reflected upon, it appears as the web of delusion regarding multiplicity.

It binds all living beings; therefore, one should remain in every state of existence with uninterrupted contemplation (*parāmarśa*), so that, having realized that the entities of the world have as their ultimate reality a single subject (*ekapramātṛ-paramārthatva*), one may no longer be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).
Thus it has been said: "In this way, the awakened one should remain at all times."
This has been explained in the *Vṛtti* by the passage beginning with "awakened, with uncontracted power. (14)

125) Now, in this way, the Supreme Lord, being the one single reality who is his own self established by himself, sports while manifesting himself through his own power of *māyā* as distinct for each individual soul (*paśu*). Thus it is in reality.

Establishing precisely the non-existence of a second category of entities, he speaks in order to demonstrate his play with the expansion of powers (*śakti*) by means of explaining the nature of the "bound soul" (*paśu*):
[He describes] the state of being an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).
Having lost his power through the loss of his *kalās*, he who has gone [to that state] is known as a bound soul (*paśu*). || 15 ||

By this extensive exposition, it has been established that the very Self, whose true nature is to be realized, is the Lord; yet, due to the reason about to be stated—namely, that all its functions are dependent on another—it is traditionally known as the *paśu* (the bound soul), which is for the most part like an animal. Because the play and worldly activity of *saṃsāra* is beginningless, it remains ever-present as something being remembered. Being of what nature [is it]? It is as follows: [text fragment].

126) Having had his power eclipsed by *kalā* and having become an object of experience, he [is related] to the supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śaktiḥ*)— which, according to the intended meaning of the expansion of the form of speech (*vāk*) to be described hereafter, consists of the collection of phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*.

The opposite of that—[the word "opposite" (viparītam) occurs here, but the remaining portion of the commentary for this verse is missing from all available manuscripts as they have been destroyed; therefore, this explanation is inserted and presented from the *Spandapradīpikā* in order to clarify the meaning of the verse: The opposite of that is the state of being a non-sentient entity (*jaḍatvam*). This is because the nature of a sentient being (*cidrūpatā*) consists in its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), whereas the nature of a non-sentient entity is the state of being perceived by another (*paraprakāśyatva*). Furthermore, this [state of being a non-sentient entity] is characterized by the absence of agency (*kartṛtva-śūnyatva*). This is because agency belongs to the conscious subject (*pramātṛ*), while non-agency belongs to the object (*prameya*). Moreover, this [non-agency] is characterized by the absence of the power of action (*kriyāśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of action belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of action belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of action] is characterized by the absence of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of knowledge belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of knowledge belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of knowledge] is characterized by the absence of the power of will (*icchāśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of will belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of will belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of will] is characterized by the absence of the power of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of sovereignty belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of sovereignty belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of sovereignty] is characterized by the absence of the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of bliss belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of bliss belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of bliss] is characterized by the absence of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of consciousness belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of consciousness belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of consciousness] is characterized by the absence of the power of existence (*sattāśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of existence belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of existence belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of existence] is characterized by the absence of the power of manifestation (*unmeṣaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of manifestation belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of manifestation belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of manifestation] is characterized by the absence of the power of contraction (*nimeṣaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of contraction belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of contraction belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of contraction] is characterized by the absence of the power of expansion (*vikāsaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of expansion belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of expansion belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of expansion] is characterized by the absence of the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāraśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of withdrawal belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of withdrawal belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of withdrawal] is characterized by the absence of the power of emission (*visargaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of emission belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of emission belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of emission] is characterized by the absence of the power of creation (*sṛṣṭiśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of creation belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of creation belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of creation] is characterized by the absence of the power of maintenance (*sthitīśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of maintenance belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of maintenance belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of maintenance] is characterized by the absence of the power of dissolution (*layaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of dissolution belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of dissolution belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of dissolution] is characterized by the absence of the power of concealment (*tirodhānaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of concealment belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of concealment belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of concealment] is characterized by the absence of the power of grace (*anugrahaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of grace belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of grace belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of grace] is characterized by the absence of the power of omniscience (*sarvajñatvaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of omniscience belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of omniscience belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of omniscience] is characterized by the absence of the power of omnipotence (*sarvakartṛtvaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of omnipotence belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of omnipotence belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of omnipotence] is characterized by the absence of the power of universal sovereignty (*sarveśvaratvaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of universal sovereignty belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of universal sovereignty belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of universal sovereignty] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme lord (*parameśvaraśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme lord belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme lord belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of the power of the supreme lord] is characterized by the absence of the power of the absolute (*anuttaraśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the absolute belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the absolute belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of the power of the absolute] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme (*parāśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of the power of the supreme] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme goddess (*parādevīśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme goddess belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme goddess belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of the power of the supreme goddess] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme reality (*paratattvaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme reality belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme reality belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of the power of the supreme reality] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme principle (*paratattvatvaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme principle belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme principle belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of the power of the supreme principle] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme state (*paradaśāśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme state belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme state belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of the power of the supreme state] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme light (*paraprakāśaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme light belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme light belongs to the object. Moreover, this [absence of the power of the supreme light] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme bliss (*parānandaśakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme bliss belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of the supreme bliss belongs to the object. Furthermore, this [absence of the power of the supreme bliss] is characterized by the absence of the power of the supreme consciousness (*paracid-śakti-śūnyatva*). This is because the power of the supreme consciousness belongs to the conscious subject, while the absence of the power of

The "mass of words" (*śabdarāśi*) is a collection of sounds, a group of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*), the *mātṛkā* consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, the mother of all words because it consists of phonemes. Its "great power is eclipsed" by the "parts" (*kalā*)— that is, the letters beginning with *ka*— of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) such as Brāhmī and others, which arises from that [mass of words] and consists of the groups of consonants beginning with *ka*.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in being displaced from one's own essential nature; for this very reason, the *puruṣa*, having fallen into the state of being an object of enjoyment, is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*) due to his lack of knowledge. And it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The subject is called the Lord (*pati*) with respect to those entities that are the forms of his own limbs."
Due to Māyā, the bound soul (paśu) becomes defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth, within the differentiated [categories].
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, when the knot of duality is severed, one attains the identity of the individual soul with the Supreme Self.
When this is not realized, he is called a bound soul (paśu); when it is realized, he is indeed the Lord (pati).
Thus [ends verse 15].
That loss of the essence of supreme nectar which arises from his cognition leads him to a state of lack of independence, and that [cognition] has only those [objects] as its sphere. [16]

127) The portion of the initial commentary is missing from all extant manuscript copies of the root text, having been lost just like the portion of the commentary on the preceding verse; therefore, [the following] is provided to indicate the meaning of this verse as well.
The explanation is introduced by extracting it directly from the *Spandapradīpikā* text:

"The emergence of cognition for that bound soul (*paśu*)—the arising of knowledge such as memory upon perceiving objects through the channels of hearing and so forth—is itself the 'loss' or 'fall' from the nectar of the Supreme, which is the rising of one's own true nature; for that [cognition]..."

By that [desire], the person attains a lack of independence, dependence on others, non-omnipresence, and so forth; and that [desire] arises from conditions, has the subtle elements as its domain, has objects such as sound as its range, and consists of longing for them—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
The person, who is not independent and whose every desired object depends upon an external collection of means, attains that state [of liberation].
This occurs when all cognitions—whether in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep—are comparable to those of the *sakala*, *vijñānākala*, and *pralayākala* types.
For him, the very emergence of such a realization is the supreme, unsurpassed, and imperishable nectar, which brings about the cessation of the flow of the supreme nectar.

The "essence" (*rasa*) of that [reality] is its own nature called Śiva, which consists of non-dual consciousness (*cinmaya*). Likewise, its "tasting" (*āsvāda*) consists of such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
Therefore, "departure" (*apāya*) is separation, a distinct state, or a contrary mode of being, consisting of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "this" and so forth.
This is what is implied within this statement: that of the one supreme reality alone—

which is essentially free from the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary imagined by its own will— there occurs, for the sake of providing a means for those to be benefited, an appearance of divisions consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Māyā (avidyā), likewise imagined by its own will.

That which is established as fivefold in the grammatical treatises (*prakriyāśāstra*) is stated concisely by the terms *parāmṛta* and *rasa*. Thus, the term *parāmṛta* denotes the very "I" (*aham*), as it expresses the essential nature known as Supreme Śiva, which is entirely devoid of contact with duality.
Furthermore, the word *rasa* is employed as a designator for the *tattva* of power (*śakti*) whose nature consists in that very reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*);
this is used for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of those who maintain that the *Śiva-tattva* is an absolute tranquility, devoid of reflective awareness, and almost entirely empty.
This has already been explained previously. Thus, these two *tattvas* are known as Śiva and Śakti.
That which, although non-different, is revealed by the knowers of reality through a division necessitated by the impossibility of otherwise explaining its essential nature;
and thus it has been stated by the Guru in the *Tattvagarbha-stotra*:
The Śiva-tattva was thus praised with the intention of establishing the primacy of that power (*śakti*), whose own essential nature consists of the characteristic of being an unceasing perceiver;
[she] who, in the form of non-conditioned light, is designated by the name "Śiva."
We perpetually worship you, that supreme Mother, who is designated by that name.

Thus, the principle of Śakti (Power), which is designated by those who have realized the supreme reality through such terms as "self-nature," "reflexive awareness," "universal vibration" (sāmānyaspanda), and so forth, has been explained as being denoted by synonymous words such as "unfolding" (unmeṣa) and the like. As it has been said:

O Mother Śivā, when your state as Śakti prevails within you, the stages designated by such terms as "unmeṣa" (expansion) and so forth proceed from the attainment of even slight swelling [of consciousness].
Thus [it is said]. Nor should it be thought that this state of power (śaktyavasthā) sometimes exists and sometimes does not exist due to a delusion regarding the hearing of the word "when" (yadā),

because it has been stated that the attribute (dharma) is essentially self-awareness by nature, eternal, and consists precisely of a general vibration (sāmānyaspanda), which is a certain degree of swelling (ucchūnatā).
Beyond that, even the triad of principles known as Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidya is indeed denoted by the term "supreme nectar" (parāmṛta),
because although the Supreme Lord is in reality one, [these states arise] through the power of His most wondrous sovereignty.

Because it consists of pure consciousness alone and is the self of the universe, it exists in a twofold form as both internal and external. Among these, since the external form—which is the self of the universe—has acquired its own nature by way of being the object of knowledge and the effect [of action], that single power is metaphorically designated as twofold by way of being knowledge and action. And that...

That state in which the nature of knowledge and action exists, yet remains internally in equilibrium without external manifestation—like the three *guṇas* in the unmanifest (*avyakta*) condition—is the stage of Sadāśiva. Although it consists of the forms of knowledge and action that constitute the enjoyment of the Supreme Lord, because it is inward-turned, it is characterized by *nimeṣa* (closing). However, where there is a predominance of the power of action...
The repose within the supreme sense of "I" (*parāhaṃbhāva*) for one whose outward manifestation has been withdrawn is the state of the Lord (*īśvaradaśā*). In that state,

however, through the surging of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), her outward-facing nature results in a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the external and internal, which culminates in a firm abiding within her own essential nature.

131) That is the state of knowledge (*vidyā-daśā*). In all three of these states, because they are rooted in the perception of duality, the power of *māyā*, even though it has acquired its own nature, remains within the very essence of supreme consciousness, which is characterized by the all-filling, perfectly full *ahaṃkāra*.
Because it is at rest, having subsided, it is not capable of concealing the nature of Śiva, which is replete with supreme bliss;
thus, these three words are indeed that supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*). As it has been said in the *Tattvagarbha*: "O Śivā, as you proceed in the form of knowledge and action..."
Those who know the principles have declared that the state of Sadāśiva is called "experience" (bhoga).
When you, whose power of knowledge has become subordinate and whose essence is manifest action,
then the Lordly Reality (aiśvara-tattva) attains manifestation through its functional activity.
When you become oriented toward manifestation within the Supreme,
you, as the noble power of knowledge, are celebrated as Vidyā.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"In this way, the activity that functions internally and externally follows the succession of time;
yet for the Subject alone, cognition and action are mutually inseparable."
However, due to the predominance of the internal state, the reality called *sādākhya* arises first;
but when there is a predominance of external existence, the reality of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*) arises subsequently.
Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), and Sadāśiva is the internal withdrawal (nimeṣa);
the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the cognitions "I" and "this" is Sadvidyā.
For those things endowed with the nature of "this-ness" that have entered the sphere of the knowable,
because their essence is consciousness, they are perceived exactly as they are.

Beyond that, however, it is solely the power of Māyā belonging to the Lord—which serves as the locus for the manifestation of His universal sovereignty—that unfolds within the state of being a *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). This state is characterized by the conceit of a self restricted to various distinctions, based on the perception of a "I" that exists through mutual exclusion and whose objects are thus divided. Consequently, one remains ignorant of one's own true sovereignty.
As it is said in the *Tattvagarbha* itself:
"When, in this state, the bound soul (paśu) possesses such innate ignorance regarding the command of enjoyment,
then you, the locus of sovereign power, are sung as being of the nature of Māyā."
Thus [it is said]. Even in recognition (pratyabhijñā), when difference shines as a single essence, and the non-self is perceived through the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā): (p. 133)
In the void of either consciousness or the body, the power of illusion unfolds.

Thus, she is designated here by the term "arising from cognition" (*pratyayodbhava*). For the perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of one's own nature as Śiva—expressed as "I am"—is precisely this;
and the power called *māyā* is declared to be the capacity of that very same nature, appearing in the form of the universe, to delineate "this-ness" (*idantā*) and thereby manifest duality.

But there is no other entity whatsoever. Furthermore, because an object being referred to as "this" cannot exist otherwise than by transcending its state of manifestation, these forms of difference are Māyā; yet, since they do not transcend their nature as attributes of the Supreme Lord whose essence is Light, they are indeed the power (*śakti*) of the Blessed One.
This is truly marvelous that He, whose very nature is such, has established Himself in this way:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion."
Thus; for this is the meaning here: "This is my divine *māyā*, belonging to the Lord (*deva*), who finds his sole delight in such playful sport.

What is the nature of that which is related to the existent as its power (*śakti*)? It is dependent on the qualities (*guṇa*). The qualities—consisting of pleasure and so forth, designated as *sattva* and the rest—are its material cause. For it has the nature of manifesting differentiation, and the differentiated object consists of the domains of sound and so forth; and the object, in turn, culminates in the experience of pleasure and the like.
It cannot be easily transcended by even those who are awakened and exert themselves to cross beyond it,
because for them there is no immediate possibility of uprooting all the conditions of worldly existence, and because the conventional practice of dualistic distinction is difficult to overcome.
Rather, it is only those who take refuge in Me— those who are truly awakened, whose consciousness is established in the state where duality has been severed— who can do so.

Those who recognize me alone as the single reality through non-dual identification with their own self have attained my own state and transcend this [illusion]. For in that condition— which shines like the light of day— this [illusion], whose very nature has been utterly destroyed, is transcended by them just as the night is by the sun.
It is as stated in the *Stotra*:
"The mountain of duality is indestructible even by others, such as Samādhivajra."
And those who possess the strength of devotion to you, though seized, are not destroyed.

Thus, it is taught here that [the world] arises solely from such conditions (*pratyaya*), and its root is the principle of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), which is expressed by the term "dependent" (*asvatantra*) as a synonym for "bound soul" (*paśu*). For this *māyā*, whose nature is the arising of conditions, causes him— who has been displaced from his true nature— to fall under the fivefold bond (*pāśapañcaka*) consisting of time and so forth, which are the prolific offspring of that *māyā* and are contrary to his essential qualities.

The state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is manifested as the dependence of that which is fettered. And thus: this [soul], deluded by this [power], failing to reflect upon its own nature (*svadharma*)—which consists of being unconditioned and so forth—is [bound] by that which is its opposite: namely, by that called Time (*kāla*), which is of the nature of limitation (*avacchedaka*), consisting of the act of mental construction (*kalana*), and divided by conceptualizations such as past, future, and so on. Furthermore...

Due to the forgetting of the attribute of being the self of all, by means of that which is called *niyati*— characterized by a fixed relationship between cause and effect everywhere— and likewise due to indifference toward the two attributes consisting of omniscience and omnipotence,
[the soul functions] through the forms of limited agency and limited knowledge.
136) [This occurs] through what are termed *kalā* and *vidyā*, due to the absence of the desired object,
because of the failure to reflect upon one's own essential nature characterized by eternal desirelessness, and by means of that which is called *rāga*, consisting of the longing for sense objects.

Bound by the noose, the *paśu* (bound soul), whose mode of existence is dependent on another, is fettered. This fivefold manifestation (*prasava*) of the power of *māyā* remains established by uniformly veiling the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entire multitude of *paśus*. However, that which transforms into the diverse forms of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth in each individual living being, it is that [specific manifestation] which veils him.
He explains the expansion of the manifestation called *pradhāna* by means of demonstrating the objects arising from cognition, stating:
"And that has the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as its domain. That arising of cognition, which is the cause of the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*), has the subtle elements as its domain;
those subtle elements—the universals such as sound and so forth—are its domain or object. For this cognition is distinct from the object of cognition (*pratyeya*).

It manifests in dependence upon an object, and the relationship between object and subject is established only when there is this triad consisting of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped. Furthermore, even that triad does not exist without a common cause for its activity.
It may be so. By this sentence, that tetrad is implied. In this context, the perceiver is the conscious individual soul (*paśu*);

the objects of perception (*grāhya*) are primarily sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—qualities (*guṇa*) characterized as specific (*viśeṣa*) and residing in the gross elements such as ether, since it is through them that all objects are perceived. And their inclusion here is appropriate, given that they exist within the general category (*sāmānya*).
The inclusion of all specific qualities is effected by the word *tanmātra* (merely-that), which denotes the general class;

by these [tanmātras], such as sound and the rest, the gross elements—ether and the others—which serve as their substrata, are implied, because those [qualities] cannot exist without a substratum. This is the tenfold effect (*kārya*). And that [subject] is the bound soul (*paśu*), who possesses cognition and is dependent on another.

Being a subject, it requires an instrument for the activity of rejecting or accepting objects that are desired or undesired. In that process, that by which one determines the object is the instrument called *buddhi*, which has illumination as its primary function; and that by which one conceives the non-self, such as the body and so forth, as being the self, is of the nature of error (*viparyaya*).

That which is called *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense), characterized primarily by restraint (*niyama*), and by means of which one does not conceptualize objects within the sphere of activity (*pravṛtti*)—that is designated as the mind (*manas*), whose nature is doubt.

Thus, the threefold internal organ has been described as the effect in successive order. That by which one perceives sound and the other objects is the fivefold group of sensory organs, beginning with the ear. That by which one performs actions such as speaking is the fivefold group of motor organs, beginning with speech—thus is the tenfold external organ. And that...

This was stated precisely because of the suffering caused by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Thus, this internal and external instrument (*karaṇa*)—this group of twenty-three effects and instruments—is implied here because it would otherwise be impossible for there to be an object of experience.
Likewise, since there can be no engagement with objects in the absence of a motivating cause, the status of being an object is established; thus he [says]:

In this context, the cause—which consists of pleasure and so forth and is designated as *pradhāna* (the primal nature)—is implied. To explain: pleasure is the satisfaction of every living being resulting from the attainment of desired objects in accordance with their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it is a transient bliss, and being impelled by it, one engages in the acquisition of desired objects. Its opposite is pain, which is a lack of fulfillment; therefore, one acts to avoid undesired objects.

But delusion (*moha*) is the state of mutual subordination between the two; when that exists, [the world] becomes established. Thus, even in its state of transformation (*vikārāvasthā*), it consists of the three qualities (*guṇa*) designated as *sattva* and so forth—having the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—for the sake of illumination, activity, and restraint, because they are mutually inseparable.
p.

139) There is only one [principle] called Pradhāna, which follows after its own manifold expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the effects and instruments that take various forms in accordance with the diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of all living beings.

With this very intention, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) employed the synonym "consisting of the desire for form and so forth" (*rūpādyabhilāṣātmaka*) for the phrase "and that has as its object only those [aggregates]" (*sa ca tanmātragocaraḥ*). It consists of that because it is caused by that desire (*abhilāṣa*), which is attachment (*rāga*), directed toward form and the other [sensory objects].
Therefore, arising from conditions, it is precisely the proliferation of desire (*abhilāṣa-prapañca*) that constitutes the primary cause consisting of pleasure and so forth;

this is the twenty-fourfold principle of the Pradhāna school, which is implied by the statement "that [cause] has the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as its object. Furthermore, twelve principles have been determined previously, namely: the five beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā, and Māyā.

The pentad beginning with Time (kālādi-pañcaka) and the principle of the bound soul (paśu-tattva)— thus, the supreme Lord’s single power unfolds as the thirty-six principles. This has already been largely explained in the commentary on page 140.
"Fall" means falling away or deviation from one's own nature, which consists of the supreme nectar-essence;
and so forth. || 16 ||

Thus, having established that for one who arises from conditions, the state of being a bound soul (paśu) consists in the causal condition of [the powers], it is said: "The bound soul is so called because he has become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers. To resolve the contradiction with what was stated previously, [the author] says: "And his powers are ever-active in obscuring his true nature."
For there is no arising of cognition without the interpenetration of words. || 17 ||

For this very self (*ātman*), whose state of being an animal (*paśutva*) has been produced by such a notion, there occurs an obscuration of its own nature—that is, an obscuration of its essential being (*svabhāva*) which consists of Śiva—due to the sole cause of the absence of such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). This constitutes a separation or a veiling; and for that reason, the previously mentioned powers (*śaktayaḥ*), which are ever-arisen because the transaction between the Lord (*pati*) and the bound soul (*paśu*) never ceases, [operate].

Constantly and perpetually aroused—that is, risen—because of the attainment of lack of independence; for [the mind] has been established as arising from conditions (*pratyayodbhava*) by virtue of being the cause for the loss of the essence of immortality.
The ellipsis is: "It cannot exist without being permeated by sound, without being intermingled with sound. If it is asked, "Why is this so?
it is said in response: Sound, indeed, consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*);
[it arises] from something other than the object, which consists of mere manifestation (*avabhāsa*).

Due to its distinction from insentient objects—such as a sword, water, or a mirror—which internally encompass a multitude of various things, [the light of consciousness] is indeed its own innate nature.
And thus, the Pratyabhijñā school knows that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the manifestation is its very nature; otherwise, it would not be so.
Even though light is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well:
"There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by language."
Thus, that which rests upon the primary meaning— consisting of the pure light of consciousness devoid of all limitations—
is called *pratyavamarśa* (reflective awareness).
It is the apprehension of the object which, though consisting of the universe, appears as diverse forms delimited by various distinctions such as genus, quality, action, and the like.
Form (*rūpa*) established as that convention (*saṃketa*)—namely, the object consisting of a specific sound (*dhvani*) perceivable by the ear—is generally designated as "word" (*śabda*). (p. 142)

Therefore, the powers (*śakti*) themselves—which have attained the form of sound (*śabda-rūpatā*), which are the very life-force arising from cognition (*pratyaya-udbhava-prāṇabhūta*), and which are ever-exerted in veiling His true nature—are what constitute the bondage. Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction with the previously stated definition: "The bound soul (*paśu*) is so called because he has fallen into the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*) for the group of powers."
This has been explained in the commentary by the words "in the veiling of one's own form, of one's own nature," and so forth. || 17 ||

Then, having first established the non-difference between this expansion culminating in sound and the supreme power, he says the following in order to demonstrate that bondage and liberation are based solely on the non-recognition of its true nature:
"This very power, whose essence is action, belonging to Śiva, resides in the bound soul (paśu)."
She who binds [the breath], abides in her own path, and when known, brings about accomplishment. || 18 ||
She is the very activity of Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who is one's own essential nature; her body consists of the operation characterized by the reflective awareness of that very nature.

Power (*śakti*) is an unfailing attribute consisting of capacity; this power, which has been described as having the nature of expansion, is none other than the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, which consists of the reflective awareness of the non-dual nature of pure consciousness (*advayacinmātra*). It is that very same [power] which, having expanded in this manner, manifests. In reality, there is no difference between her and him—this is the meaning. As it has been said:
In that state, there exists no portion of the individual soul (jīva-kalā) residing within either of the two continuums,
nor is there any all-pervading portion of Śiva (śiva-kalā) that acts as its presiding controller.

Thus [it is said]. For this is the meaning of the verse: for the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a bound person (*paśu*), there is a twofold continuity of the *kalās*—consisting of the nature of knowledge and the nature of action. Among these, that which consists of knowledge is of the nature of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and is threefold;
that which consists of action is of the nature of the external organs (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) and, together with the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) abiding in its own nature, is elevenfold.
The fourteen-fold continuum of the *jīva-kalā* is, in summary, truly twofold;
there is no other *kalā* of the living self (*jīva-ātman*) existing apart from these two continua. This is the remainder [of the sense].

Within this [twofold continuum], the Pervasive One—the Sovereign whose glory is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth—presides over everything by presiding over it through its state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and other such attributes.

Having made [the world] dependent upon itself, the *śivakalā*—the supreme power (*parā śakti*) which is a digit (*kalā*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self—exists; it does not exist in the form previously described. (p. 144) Its existence is as follows:

The meaning is that she herself deviates [from her own nature] while appearing in this way. Even amidst manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*), because the pervasive attribute of Śiva—the universal form characterized by manifestation—is never obscured, this very Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) appears as the Non-Supreme (*aparā*) in the form of gross activity; thus, the ultimate reality is precisely the non-difference between the Supreme and the Non-Supreme powers.
Thus it has been made known. This very point is also stated in the *Jñānagarbha-stotra*:
"O Caṇḍikā, by whichever of the fourteen paths one may travel—whether they be the external organs, the intellect, the ego, the mind, or the Suṣumnā—"
O Mother, that digit which is the abode of Śiva—ten such digits arise there, which are indeed difficult to attain in this world even for the gods.

The intended meaning of this verse is as follows: the fivefold group beginning with the ear, the fivefold group beginning with speech—these constitute the tenfold external organs; the threefold internal organ consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*);
and the central vital breath (*madhyama-prāṇa*). These are the fourteen divisions of *kalā*, which is the power whose essence is consciousness (*cid-ātmikā*). Of these...
Among all those very many paths and avenues of expansion, by whichever single path among them this *kalā* [proceeds] to the abode of Śiva—
The connection is as follows: "Śiva, the Supreme Self, would go; He alone is the abode and the temple; one should go there"—thus the state arises.

"One should go to the abode of Śiva" means that the ultimate function of the *kalā* consists in taking refuge in one's own state called Śiva, which is distinct from the perception of duality belonging to *māyā*; this is established as a matter of fact.

This art (kalā) has been discussed. For it arises from its own locus, which is identical with Śiva and whose definition has been established by such statements as "neither suffering nor pleasure," and having fulfilled its purpose, it finally enters back into that very source and becomes of one flavor (samarasībhavati), like a river into the ocean;
even in the interim, it exists in a state of multiplicity through the nature of the mutually distinct expansions of the intellect (buddhi) and the other faculties.

Even while appearing as the form of water, it does not deviate from its nature as consciousness, just as [water] does not deviate from its nature as a universal; thus, it never departs from the essential nature of Śiva, yet it is simply not recognized as such by those deluded by the power of Māyā.
In this way, by whichever path this *kalā* may travel toward the abode of Śiva...

In that regard, such a state— being self-evident and thus impossible to describe to anyone else— arises and is manifested for one who is truly awakened; it is a condition difficult even for the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to attain, for they [are not yet awakened].

Because they do not transcend the animal-like conceit (pāśavābhimāna) delimited by [notions] such as Brahmanhood produced by the arising of conditions, how could they attain the state of the Lord (patidaśā), which is the very form of Śiva? Now, the subject at hand is explained: however, even though she is of this nature, this supreme power of the Supreme Lord, whose essence is action (kriyātmikā), resides within the bound soul (paśu) as its binder.

Residing in the *paśu*— the individual soul (*puruṣa*) who has attained a state of dependence through the arising of the cognition of duality— it is the agent of *saṃsāra*, which consists of bondage and the continuous revolution of births and so forth. For the *paśu*, indeed, determines this [power] as his own property, [identifying it] with the self that is entirely delimited.

Because its own cognitive activity (*jñānakriyā*) consists merely in the experience of pleasure and so forth produced by the acquisition of desired objects and the avoidance of undesired ones, it does not touch upon that ultimate reality (*tat-paramārtha*) and thus differentiates [it]. And that [reality], being grasped as thus differentiated, [persists] until the dawning of awakening.
"By means of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), she binds"—thus it is said that she abides as the binder within the bound soul. Now, [one might ask]:
"In this way—[she is] known, understood, and recognized through the nature of the activity of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) of one's own essential nature, which consists of Śiva."
Satī is the bringer-about of accomplishment (*siddhi*); she is the producer of the higher accomplishment characterized by the attainment of self-sovereignty (*ātmaiśvarya*),

and the means for the manifestation of various incidental powers (*vibhūti*)— the lower accomplishment— since, by the power of her own essential nature, she brings these about when she abides in her own path within herself.

The meaning is that she stands on the path whose nature is Śiva, with her movement turned away from other objects distinct from Him; however, in relation to the perceived duality manifested by the power of Māyā arising from the emergence of limited cognition, she is called the "portion of the individual soul" (jīvakalā) residing in the state of a bound animal (paśu).
But for one whose awakening has arisen, all [these states] are recognized as they truly are.
She brings about the accomplishments (*siddhi*). Having thus explained the meaning of the verse, she is now established as being situated on her own path, as will be demonstrated. She (p.

Indeed, it has been demonstrated many times by the Supreme Lord in the scriptures that the supreme Śakti herself, whose nature consists solely in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the manifestation of the Supreme Lord’s own essence, has issued forth in the form of speech (*vāk*); thus, His constant abiding on His own path has been established for her. And so it is stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijaya*:
O Goddess, that power of the Creator of the universe which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) becomes His will when He desires to emit [the world].
Listen to how even that which is one attains multiplicity:
it should be understood with firm certainty that "it is thus, and not otherwise."
When she makes known [the will] here in this world, saying "let all this be so," being intent upon the task, she is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
At that very moment, the action is considered to be performed in such a manner;
thus, while it is essentially of two forms, it again attains multiplicity through its various divisions.
Under the influence of the limiting adjuncts of objects, the Sovereign Goddess becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem;
having first entered therein into the state of the Mother, she then diversifies herself.

This meaning has been elucidated by such passages as: "Mālinī is twofold, ninefold through its divisions, and fiftyfold," and so forth; likewise, even by those who maintain the non-duality of sound (śabdādvayavādins).
By those who demonstrate its expansion through the method of discursive expression (*vivṛtti-vācoyukti*), it is shown that this [consciousness] remains precisely within its own path. As they say:
"If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from cognition..."
For that [consciousness] alone, which possesses reflective awareness, would illuminate the light.

Thus, this is that state of absolute non-duality in which her own abiding in her own path is perfectly manifest. When, however, she withdraws—due to a lack of reflective awareness—the entire universe that flashes forth within her as "this," with its manifold forms, divisions, and succession, and rests for a moment in the sky of her own nature, which is her own majesty devoid of division and sequence; [then she is said to be in that state].

At that time, there remains only the manifestation of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); this is described as the unfolding of the inner, supreme knower in the form of speech designated as *paśyantī*. As they say:
"But *paśyantī* is undivided, with all sequential order withdrawn from every side."
The light of one’s own true nature alone is the subtle, inseparable speech within.

Thus it is said. Here too, this [power] remains within its own domain; for, apart from the effort of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it exists in each living being as the nature of specific sounds that have arisen within the body and are without beginning or end.

When she follows the sequence of time and so forth, as well as the division of phonemes and so forth, and assumes an expansion, she is then called the manifestation whose form is speech known as the *madhyamā*; even then, not transcending her nature as pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), she remains established on her own path. As it has been said:
Taking up the intellect as its substrate and following the sequence of forms,
the middle speech (madhyamā vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus [it is said]. But when the wind called *prāṇa*, impelled by an effort that conforms to the desire of the person who utters [the speech],

undergoes a collision within the regions of the body such as the chest and so forth, that very same general sound (*sāmānyadhvani*)— even though there is a difference among the speakers— assumes the form of specific phonemes (*varṇa*) determined by their shapes and so on, which are divided into the distinctions of vowels, consonants, and the like.

It has been stated that, at that time, there occurs an unerring expansion in the form of speech designated as *vaikharī*, which rests upon the mere vital breath (*prāṇa*) that manifests distinctions such as phonemes (*varṇa*).
As it has been said:

"Vaikharī speech, which assumes the form of articulated phonemes, occurs when the vital air is struck against the [articulatory] sites; it is dependent upon the activity of the breath of the speakers."

Thus, even then, this [speech]—not abandoning its nature as a collection of phonemes that are immutable and fixed despite the diversity of place, time, substratum, speaker, and so forth, and whose manifestation depends on human will and other factors—is indeed eternal;
and even in this state of *madhyamā*, the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatva*) remains continuous. Thus, it also abides within its own path.

Her [nature] is not obstructed. Thus, although she has attained the form of *vaikharī*, she assumes an infinite expansion through the distinctions of the groups of letters (*mātṛkā*), individual phonemes, words, and sentence-meanings. And just as this [expansion] is infinite in its flow when taking the form of *varṇa-vaikharī*, so too is it when taking the form of *svara-vaikharī*.

Furthermore, it has an infinite expansion through the distinctions of notes (*svara*), scales (*grāma*), melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*), musical intervals (*tāna*), and the resulting melodies (*rāga*) and so forth. Thus, this is the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of the Supreme Lord.
Although she has issued forth by her own infinite majesty— beginning with the act of self-reflection upon intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extending to conventional words—

she never deviates from remaining on her own path, for she is the reflector of the entire range of objects whose very acquisition of self-nature is impossible apart from the light of universal consciousness (*sāmānyasaṃvit*).

And therefore— although bound by various forms of conceptualization produced by the power of *māyā* manifested by the Lord for the sake of the world’s play, those whose vision of pure consciousness is skilled in grasping that true nature [of reality] through the awakening brought about by contact with the power of grace;

It is simply impossible to completely veil or conceal [the Self] from the perceivers by means of those [impurities], as it has been said: "Though this [Self] is constantly being overwhelmed by adventitious impurities,
it is not utterly overcome, just like the final digit of the moon."
Thus, it is established that the Supreme Cause itself has thus issued forth even in the form of divided sound:
"The Truth (Satya) is supreme, subtle, faultless, and unsurpassed."
Then the supreme Brahman, which is absolute peace, attained the state of being the primordial phoneme.

(153) and so forth. Likewise, in the doctrine of the non-duality of word and meaning (*śabdādvayavāda*), that which is the expansion of the Lord’s power (*śaktiprasara*)— which, in its general form, consists of both word and meaning and possesses infinite internal subdivisions— [is to be understood].
He proceeded with his discourse by means of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). As he said:
"Now, this internal knower, abiding in the subtle self of speech, undergoes an illusory manifestation as sound (*śabda*) for the sake of manifesting its own form."
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of speech, the imperishable syllable;
from it proceeds the evolution of the world through the manifestation of objects.
Thus, here, by virtue of being the reality of the word that is synonymous with Brahman, the very form of the Supreme Lord is indicated. It has been stated:

"This supreme power (*parā śakti*), when abiding in her own path, being known and having her true nature correctly realized, brings about complete perfection. This very [power], having attained the state of *vaikharī* (the manifest speech),...
The gross power of action (*sthūlā kriyāśakti*) is said in some places to have its manifestation dependent upon the vibration of the vital breaths of the person;
prior to that is the intermediate speech (*madhyamā vāk*), which is the power of will (*icchāśakti*); and prior to that is the *paśyantī*.
"Knowledge-power" (jñānaśakti). Thus, being a power, she requires a possessor of power;

her locus is the divine form (vigraha) which is non-different from Mātṛkā, consisting of the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), and primarily characterized by the power of action (kriyāśakti), wherein this [universe] unfolds through its own various expansions, beginning with the consonant groups (varga) and ending with sentences.

Furthermore, its manifestation in the form of speech is twofold, distinguished as eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). Among these, that which consists of *mantras* and that which consists of *śāstras* is eternal; however, that which consists of worldly sentences pertaining to the sphere of mundane transaction is non-eternal. Thus, this manifestation consisting of speech, when recognized as the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, bestows supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*).
However, when delimited by its connection to various sacrificial animals, it becomes a cause of bondage;
this has been explained in the *Vṛtti*,
and this [power] consists of action, having the nature of action.
By [the passage] beginning with "ityādi" || 18 ||

Having thus established that the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is manifested by one's own *māyā* within the very essence of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is identical to the Lord (*pati*), [the author] now explains how this same [Self], while existing as a bound soul, becomes recognized as standing upon its own path through the arising of knowledge (*vidyodaya*).

The Supreme Power (parā śaktiḥ), by manifesting as the state of being the Lord (patitva), is the cause for the cessation of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Announcing his intention to state the reason—preceded by an exposition of the causes of transmigratory existence—he speaks these two verses:
"By means of that which consists of the emergence of the subtle elements (tanmātra), and which functions as the mind (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), and intellect (buddhi)..."
Constrained by the city of eight, [the self] experiences that which arises from the resulting cognitions. (19)
He experiences enjoyment under the control of another; because of that state, he wanders through saṃsāra.
Therefore, we shall now explain the cause for the dissolution of this saṃsāra.
