In the subtle body, there are the five *tanmātras* and the three *guṇas*; thus, these eight constitute the cause of the gross body. (p. 156)

That which is situated [within] is the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which is the face [of the self]; because it is its effect, even the gross body is here referred to by that term, "the city of eight. Bound by that, identifying itself as being merely that much, and due to the power of forgetting its own capacity for universal selfhood and so forth, it is bound; for this very reason, it is dependent on another.
Because the accomplishment of all desired objects depends upon other causes distinct from his own nature, which consists of all powers, he is not independent; thus, while experiencing enjoyment—
which consists of the perception of pleasure and so forth in accordance with the latent impressions accumulated by his own beginningless karma manifested through *māyā*— he remains dependent.
It experiences—that is, it undergoes—the object of its own domain once that [process] has reached its conclusion. Of what nature is that?

It is "arisen from that," meaning it has emerged from that *puryaṣṭaka*; for indeed, the accomplishment of experience is possible only when there is a bond with a body. What is that experience? It is "the arising of cognition."

The meaning is as follows: experience (*bhoga*) consists precisely in the arising of a cognition whose nature is fixed by the previously explained form [of the object] and which has its own object as its domain; that is, the arising of a mental state characterized by the conceit of being the enjoyer of its own object alone.
By what kind of *puryaṣṭaka* (eightfold subtle body) is he bound? By that which consists in the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The subtle elements (tanmātras), such as sound and the rest, are manifested by the will of the Lord alone as the causal basis for the gross elements (p. 157).

Their emergence (*udaya*) is their manifestation as the ether and other elements transformed into the state of the gross body. And thus: herein, whatever is a cavity such as the channels (*nāḍī*) is the ether, the emergence of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*); whatever is active, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is air, the emergence of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*); and whatever has the nature of heat, luminosity, and so forth, such as fire, is fire.
The emergence of the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) is whatever has a liquid nature, such as blood and so forth—that is water, the emergence of the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*).

Whatever is solid, such as flesh, bone, sinew, and so forth—that is earth, the emergence of the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*). Thus, "having that as its form" means having as its form or configuration the emergence of the subtle elements; by that [it is so described]. Having thus explained the state of having the emergence of the subtle elements as its form:
To demonstrate that its nature consists in the emergence of qualities (*guṇodayarūpatva*), he states another qualification: "by the functions of mind, ego, and intellect" (*mano'haṃbuddhivṛttinā*).

Since the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) and the experience (*anubhava*) of this [Self] which is being experienced reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), when *rajas* emerges in the mind (*manas*), *tamas* emerges in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and *sattva* emerges in the intellect (*buddhi*), [the Self is manifested].
By one whose mode of being, conduct, and state of existence are such as described; and he, being thus constrained by the *puryaṣṭaka*, is a bound soul (*paśu*).

Because of its existence—that is, because of the presence of that subtle and gross *puryaṣṭaka*—as long as there is no awakening, due to its non-cessation, one would transmigrate incessantly, experiencing the whirling wheel of karma consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for the enjoyment of various bodies, until the dawning of awakening. This is the intended meaning here: for the person confined within a body...

The conceit of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvābhimāna*) regarding experience (*bhoga*), which consists in the perception of specific pleasure and so forth, is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, we declare that the mere abiding in one’s own stainless essential nature (*nirāvaraṇasvasvarūpasthitimātra*) is the cause for the destruction of transmigratory existence.
This has been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti*.
By the passage beginning with "the arising of the subtle elements" (tanmātrodaya),
one experiences— that is, eats— under the power of another.
And so on, as stated in verses 19 and 20.

Now, immediately after [discussing] that by which the state of being the Lord (*patitva*)— the nature of sovereignty as previously described— of Śiva himself is manifested, the author concludes the section by teaching another means (*upāya*) that was promised:
"But when [the mind] is firmly established in one [object], then its dissolution and emergence [occur]."
By restraining [the senses], one attains the state of an enjoyer; from that, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara). || 21 ||
But when, at a certain time, between these two bodies designated as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka)— which are rooted solely in the emergence of cognitive impressions—
one or the other is established as the body of the very object being experienced, according to the reasoning previously set forth; |||
Among the gross and subtle bodies, distinguished as consisting of the elements (*bhūta*) and consisting of objective entities (*bhāva*), or else—

among the gross and subtle states (*bhāva*) which are to be taken as objects of meditation (*ālambanīya*)— he is "firmly rooted" (*saṃrūḍha*) in one of them, meaning he is perfectly and without delay established therein.

(160) Through the excellence of one-pointedness, the practitioner whose consciousness has transformed into non-duality then, at that very moment, controls the dissolution and emergence— the forms of relinquishment and grasping, which are destruction and production— of that aforementioned body perceived as non-dual.

Determined that the true agent— the Self (*ātman*) which is about to be described by the word "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*)— is indeed the effect, and establishing it through non-conceptualization, one attains the state of being the enjoyer; that is, one reaches the state of the enjoyer, whose nature is that of the supreme Self as a mere perceiver, and even though it exists at that very moment, one takes possession of it through recognition.

Then, by reason of the recognition of the true nature of the Self (*satyātmasvarūpa-pratyabhijñā*), one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*); that is, by the previously explained state of the wheel, one becomes the sovereign (*īśvara*) or presiding authority over the multitude of one's own powers (*svaśaktisamūha*), which have emerged from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) and extended throughout the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) down to all moving and unmoving beings.
When [the object] is understood as being merely the unfolding of one's own sovereignty,
one becomes its disposer at will; for it is precisely then that innate freedom is manifested.

When the cognition of the animal has been destroyed, having abandoned the state of being an object of enjoyment for the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), the sovereignty consisting in the state of being its enjoyer is established; therefore, one should restrain both that dissolution and that emergence within the self as the enjoyer—this is the meaning of the sentence. This is the intended purport here: just as any embodied being whatsoever...

One whose self-conceit is established solely in the body, while exercising the acts of abandoning and grasping toward external objects such as jars—which are perceived only as objects to be grasped—determines within such a self, "I alone am the agent of these two. Thus, he considers himself to be an independent agent residing within the state of embodiment, even though his self is not actually situated in the body. Such is his conviction.

The renunciation and grasping performed by bringing the body to the state of being an object of cognition necessarily result in a restriction within one's own true Self— which, by its very nature as the unique agent, is always incapable of contact with objectivity and is established by the inherent power of reality— as something distinct from that [body].
Even though they both partake [of the same nature], because of their lack of awakening, one does not realize it; therefore,
this instruction is intended only for one whose wisdom has been awakened and who is capable of grasping the distinction between the body and the embodied self, for this reason.
Only such a person, whose knots of doubt have been shattered by the power of grace, is a fit vessel for this kind of specialized instruction from the Supreme Lord. As it is said:
"He is the source of all; from Him everything proceeds."
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me.
With their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they find contentment and delight.
To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love,
I grant that yoga of discernment by which they attain Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.

Thus, because of this instruction being practiced, immediately thereafter, there occurs the [realization] of that very body which was explained as "in one place" and which appears as non-differentiated.

The dissolution and emergence, consisting of the acts of relinquishment and grasping, which belong to that which is being made an object of knowledge, are— when governed as effects by the independence of the Supreme Lord himself, the enjoyer who possesses qualities contrary to those [of the object]— they bring about the recognition of the nature of the Controller and lead to universal sovereignty; therefore, one should restrain them there.

Since the world, including its dissolution and emergence, is non-different from His own nature, His manifestation consists of the wheel of His own powers (*sva-śakti-cakra*); thus, by fulfilling the meaning as it was initially proposed, there is only one single reality whose characteristic is never to deviate from the self-reflection of its own nature (*svarūpa-parāmarśa-mātra*). Therefore, nothing exists that is ultimately real apart from this.
This has been established as being possible. As it was said:
"In the ultimate sense, however, oneness does not have a characteristic different from separateness;
reality shines forth as a single essence in the form of both separateness and oneness."
That which is undoubtedly distinct does not differ from unity;
that which is undoubtedly one does not differ from distinctness.
Heaven, earth, wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers,
and the directions are the external manifestations of the reality of the internal organ.

Thus, this very same meaning has been set forth by us in our own hymn (*Svastotra*) through another mode of expression: "Dancing in many ways externally from her own body, yet not different within it—she whose various forms are marked by new ornaments fashioned from the conceptualizations of diverse perceptions; again,"
Victorious alone is Śambhu, who is eternally possessed of ever-new wonder as he gazes upon his own beloved power, and whose greatness of unbroken and incomparable joy is supreme.

Thus, in this verse just explained, the subject matter— the non-dual sovereignty of the Self characterized as being cognizable through self-awareness— which was promised in the opening verse of the treatise, has been brought to its conclusion. This has been explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*).
Furthermore, [this is shown] by the passage beginning with "when, however, in one [object], whether gross or subtle," and so forth. || 21 ||

Thus ends the fourth outflow (*niṣyanda*), titled "The Realization of the Non-differentiation of the Universe from the Nature of Power," along with its miscellaneous sections, in the *Spandavivṛti* composed by the venerable Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. 4.

165) Now, the sole cause for the non-manifestation of even a mere doubt regarding the single reality that is the Self is such that it cannot be uprooted except through the instruction of a true guru; for the Supreme Lord, having entered the form of the guru—

He awakens those worthy of grace by means of making them recognize their own [true nature]; thus, by way of praising his own Guru Sarasvatī, he says: "The boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt..."
I pay homage to that wondrous speech of my Guru, which is variegated with words of manifold meanings.

I bow to that speech of my Guru, named Vasugupta, which flashes forth in the heart though its true nature is impossible to fully express— the speech from which flows the nectar of the *spanda* principle, which constitutes the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all truths directly transmitted from the mouths of the perfected ones (*siddhas*).

I praise the speech of Bhāratī. Of what kind?—by the half-verse beginning with "agādha" (p. 166), the qualification is as follows: that which has no *gādha*, meaning no ground for rest (*viśrānti-bhūmikā*), is such [as that].

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is an error consisting in the non-comprehension of reality; it is an ocean because it is crowded with a web of waves of difficult-to-subdue conceptual constructions. For the purpose of crossing—that is, for the complete transcending—of that ocean, [this work serves as] a ferry-boat (*tāriṇī nāv*). Likewise, it consists of words with diverse meanings and phrases; "diverse" means most wonderful, and such are the words whose referents (*abhidheya*) are the objects (*vastu*) to be expressed.
In which [work] she [resides]; thus, he praises that "wondrous" [work], because it possesses a variety of compositions and thereby inspires amazement.

By these two adjectives, he extols both the excellence of the meaning and the excellence of the words; for herein lies a manifold meaning that is beyond the scope of the common understanding of all people, yet finds resonance in the hearts of a few world-transcending awakened ones.
And the arrangement of words and sentences is "variegated" (citrā) when it possesses the capacity to convey such meanings—thus [it is said].
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*):
for it is unfathomable, without foundation, and infinite.
By means of this and other passages in the text. || 1 ||

167) This treasure, called Spanda, has been revealed here, with the fear of the serpent of doubt dispelled; it contains within its womb the jewel of unsurpassed knowledge that bestows complete perfection.

May the supreme grace of Śaṅkara make fruitful the attainment of this [work] for the fortunate, by bestowing it upon all seekers and by causing them themselves to experience the enjoyment of innate bliss. || 1 ||
This which has been sung by me— a bee of fully ripened awakening emerging from a lofty disposition like a magnificent, expansive blue lotus that adorns the lake of the six sciences—
whom among conscious beings does it not bring forth unsurpassed joy and sweetness for one who listens with focused attention? Rāma.
Possessing supreme rest. || 2 ||

When the mind becomes agitated by some base object, one should remain silent and steady it; then, having turned back that agitation through affection and gradually propitiated one's own beloved consciousness,
one should kiss her incessantly, with eyes closed from the throbbing of a fresh bliss arising from a dense embrace in which the boundaries between self and other have dissolved.
May you possess auspicious intentions. || 3 ||
If there is anything here that has been over-stated, or even left unsaid, or whatever has been poorly expressed,
let it be disregarded by the wise whose intellects are solely intent on discerning subtle details.
Do those in the forest who are eager for the taste of the essence-drops of nectar within a flower ever find [the scent]?
Just as bees [are repelled] by the touch of the tips of hard thorns. || 4 ||
That darkness which once rendered the entire world motionless and could not be dispelled by the moon, the stars, lamps, and the like—
now that it has met its destruction through the arrival of the stainless sun, let those who have achieved their purpose cast off their contraction and awaken.
Visible to people. || 5 ||
Victorious is Bhavānī, who delivers people from misfortune; victorious is the Enemy of Smara, by whose own splendor the universe is pervaded;
and victorious is that Elephant-faced One, by whose grace the entire host of obstacles and calamities comes to rest. (6)
This *Spandavivṛti*, following the commentary (*vṛtti*), is complete.
It is the work of [Abhinavagupta],
who dwells at the lotus feet of the venerable Rājānaka Śrī Utpaladeva— the crest-jewel of the great Maheśvara teachers and a follower of both [the Lord and his consort].
This is the work of Rājānaka Śrī Rāmakaṇṭha; may there be auspiciousness!
